en: The Sūtra of the Buddha-treasury, Volume One; Entitled *The Sūtra of the Dragon Flower*, also known as *The Selection of All Dharmas*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: The True Reality of All Dharmas (Part One). Chapter One: The True Reality of All Dharmas.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, all of whom were well-known to the public, as well as an infinite multitude of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, immeasurable and innumerable.
At that time, Śāriputra arose from samādhi, went to where the Buddha was, bared his right shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
"The Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, so as to cause people to believe and understand them.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"What benefit do you see that leads you to exclaim how rare it is that the Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, so as to cause people to believe and understand them?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
While staying in a quiet place, I have often had this thought:"
"The World-Honored One teaches by means of names and signs that which is without name or sign; he teaches by means of speech that which is beyond speech.
Reflecting on this matter, a sense of rare wonder arose within him.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!
This matter is rare, the foremost rarity; namely, this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas.”
Śāriputra! It is as if a skilled painter were to paint various forms and colors in empty space.
What do you think?
"Is such a painter rare or not? "Rare,
World-Honored One!"

“Śāriputra! That the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and teaches that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, causing people to believe and understand this, is doubly rare.”
Why is this? Because there are no dharmas with names or marks;

there is no thought, no attainment, and no cultivation; it is inconceivable, not that upon which the mind relies, and free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), nor is it that which can be relied upon by conceptual proliferation.

Without applied thought or sustained reflection, without anything grasped, not residing in the mind, and neither attained nor non-attained; without "this" or "that," without discrimination, without movement or intrinsic nature, primordially empty by nature; it cannot be conceived and cannot be transcended, and is something that all the world cannot believe. Thus, this dharma which is without name or characteristic is explained by means of names and characteristics.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
That all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, and that one can cause others to believe and understand this, is doubly rare.
“Śāriputra! Suppose there were a person who could chew and swallow Mount Sumeru until it was completely exhausted, and who could fly through space without suffering any harm. What do you think?”
“Is it rare? “It is rare,
World-Honored One!”

“Śāriputra! That all dharmas spoken by the Buddhas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, and that they cause people to believe and understand this, is doubly rare.”

Śāriputra! Suppose there were a city of fire, one yojana in length, breadth, and depth, with flames issuing from its four gates. A person carrying dry grass on their back were to pass through it; though fierce winds blow the flames so that they scorch and explode against their body, this person is able to prevent the fire from burning the grass or the body, emerging from within as if nothing had happened.
"What do you think?
Is this rare or not? "It is rare."
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!
That the Tathāgata’s teaching that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, causes people to believe and understand it—this is doubly rare.”
Śāriputra! Suppose there were a person who used a raft made of stone to cross from this shore of the ocean to the other shore.
What do you think?
“Is it rare? “It is rare,
World-Honored One!”
“Śāriputra! That the Tathāgata teaches that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, causing people to believe and understand this, is doubly rare.”

Śāriputra! It is as if there were a person who, carrying the four continents, the various Sumeru mountains, and the rivers, mountains, grasses, and trees, used the legs of a mosquito as a ladder to ascend to the Brahma Heaven.
"What do you think? Is this rare? “It is rare.”
“World-Honored One!

[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra, for the Tathāgata to teach that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, so as to cause people to believe and understand this—this is doubly rare.”
Śāriputra! It is as if a thread from a lotus fiber were to suspend Mount Sumeru in the midst of space.
What do you think?
“Is it rare? “It is rare,
World-Honored One!”
“Śāriputra! That the Tathāgata teaches that all dharmas are without arising or cessation, without marks, and unconditioned, causing people to believe and understand this, is doubly rare.”

Śāriputra! It is as if, when the great fire at the end of an eon is burning, a person could extinguish this fire with a single spit of saliva, and with a single breath, restore the world and all its celestial palaces.
"What do you think?
Is this rare or not? "It is rare."
“World-Honored One!
“Śāriputra! That the Tathāgata’s teaching that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, causes people to believe and understand it—this is doubly rare.”
“Śāriputra! Is the Ganges vast and immeasurable? “It is so.”
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!

Suppose it were raining heavily throughout the four continents, with drops as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and there were a person who could catch these raindrops with their hand without missing a single one.”
"What do you think?
Is this rare or not? "It is rare."
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!
That the Tathāgata’s teaching that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, causes people to believe and understand it—this is doubly rare.”
“Śāriputra, is Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, high and great?
“It is high and great.”
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!

Suppose it were raining great stones throughout the four continents, each as large as Mount Sumeru, and there were a person who could catch these stones with their hands without letting even a single one as small as a mustard seed fall.”
"What do you think? Is this rare or not?
"It is rare, World-Honored One!"

“Śāriputra! That the Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, so as to cause people to believe and understand them, is doubly rare.”

Śāriputra! It is as if there were a person who placed all sentient beings in his left hand, and with his right hand lifted up the mountains, rivers, grasses, and trees of the trichiliocosm, yet was able to cause all these sentient beings to share a single heart of joy and gladness, their minds remaining undivided.
"What do you think?
Is this rare or not? "It is rare."
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!
That the Tathāgata’s teaching that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned, causes people to believe and understand it—this is doubly rare.”
“Śāriputra! That which the Tathāgata has taught—that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature, empty, and non-existent—is difficult for the entire world to believe and understand.”

Why is this? Śāriputra! This Dharma is without perception and free from all perceptions; it is without thought and free from all thoughts; it is without grasping and without abandoning; it is without conceptual proliferation and without afflictive heat. It is not this shore, not the other shore, and not the dry land; it is neither ignorance nor clarity. It can only be understood through immeasurable wisdom; it cannot be known through discursive deliberation.

It is without activity and without marks; it is without affliction or fever; it is without thought, surpassing all thoughts; it is without mind, surpassing all minds; it is without orientation and without aversion; it is without bondage and without liberation; it is without delusion and without the phenomena of delusion; it is without the net of ignorance; it is without name and without speech; it is without teaching and without non-teaching; it is without exhaustion and without non-exhaustion; it is without practice and without the marks of practice; it is without the path and without the fruit of the path; it is without departure, surpassing all departures; it is without contemplation and without admixture; it is neither grasping nor rejecting; it is without attainment and nothing that can be attained.

It eliminates all obstructions and attachments; it removes greed, hatred, and delusion. It is neither real nor illusory, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither luminous nor non-luminous, neither dark nor illuminating. It does not reside in the mind and possesses no intrinsic nature; its nature is fundamentally empty.

It is able to subdue Māra, to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), to subdue the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), to subdue the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and to subdue the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). It subdues those who claim that the five aggregates exist, those who claim that the twelve bases exist, and those who claim that the eighteen elements exist. It subdues those who claim that there is a sentient being (*sattva*), a person (*pudgala*), a life-principle (*jīva*), a vital principle (*jantu*), an existing entity (*bhava*), or a non-existing entity (*abhava*), and it subdues all those who engage in erroneous practices.

“Śāriputra! This holy Dharma of mine is able to subdue all forms of attachment, even those who assert the existence of phenomena, those who do not believe in or delight in the true nature of all phenomena as it really is, and those who oppose the Buddha-dharma.”
Why is this so? Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who speak of a self,

who speak of a person, who speak of a sentient being, who speak of annihilation, who speak of permanence, who speak of existence, who speak of non-existence, who speak of all dharmas, who speak of provisional names, or who speak of extremes— they all oppose the Buddha and contend with the Buddha.
Śāriputra! Even those who have attained even the slightest portion of the Dharma are all contending with the Buddha;
those who contend with the Buddha have entered onto a deviant path and are not my disciples.
"If one is not my disciple, they are then in contention with Nirvana, in contention with the Buddha, in contention with the Dharma, and in contention with the Sangha. Śāriputra!"
If I see such a person, I do not permit them to leave the household life or receive the precepts. Śāriputra!
If I see such a person, I do not permit them to receive even a single drink of water as an offering for my own sustenance.

“Śāriputra! If there are those who abandon such unwholesome attachments and leave the household life within my Dharma to seek the Way, they do not think of nirvāṇa, do not take nirvāṇa as their object of thought, and do not crave nirvāṇa.”

If one is neither startled nor terrified by the dharma of ultimate emptiness, such a person still exerts diligent effort for the sake of severing all dharmas; how much more so, then, regarding such unwholesome attachments—namely, attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, attachment to a person, and attachment to dharmas.

In order to sever all attachments, this person diligently cultivates the signless samādhi; yet even within the signless samādhi, they do not grasp at signs. This person penetrates the realization that the characteristics of all dharmas are but a single characteristic, namely, signlessness.
“Śāriputra! This is what is called ‘the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma’ within the Noble Dharma.
Having attained this patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma, one is then called my disciple; such a person is able to digest offerings and does not receive this body in vain.”
Why is this so? Śāriputra!
This Dharma of my true mark is unenterable, ungraspable, and unrelinquishable; it is uncravable and unspeakable, cutting off the path of language.
Without joy and without delight, one cuts off the mind of craving and gladness; it is not a convergence of various conditions, nor is it separated from various causes and conditions.

Without a path, one cuts off the path and reaches the state beyond the path; one cuts off all speech, debate, and sounds. It is formless and colorless, without grasping, without attachment, and without utility; it is neither real nor false, neither dark nor bright, neither destruction nor contention, neither conjunction nor dispersion, neither movement nor thought, and without discrimination—it cannot be demonstrated.
It is neither defiled nor pure; it is neither name nor mark; it is not a mental factor, nor is it something to be understood by the mind.
Within this Dharma of mine, there is no male and no female;
there are no devas, no nāgas, no yakṣas, no gandharvas, no kumbhāṇḍas, and no piśācas; there is neither annihilation nor permanence.
I am without sentient beings and without persons; there is no coming and no going, no exiting and no entering;
there is no precept and no transgression, no purity and no defilement; there is no samādhi, no concentration and no faculty of concentration; there is no dhyāna and no faculty of dhyāna;
there is no knowledge and no vision, no greed and no contention; there is no path and no fruit of the path.
There is no wisdom and no faculty of wisdom; there is no ignorance and no non-ignorance; there is no liberation and no non-liberation;
there is no fruit and no attainment of fruit; there is no power and no non-power; there is no fearlessness and no non-fearlessness;
there is no mindfulness and no faculty of mindfulness; there is no sitting and no walking, nor any deportment; there is neither this nor that.
It is without recollection or conceptualization; there is no awakening and no factors of awakening; there is no wisdom and no non-wisdom;
there is no earth, no water, no fire, and no wind.

There is no sin and no merit; there is no dharma and no non-dharma; there is no suffering and no pleasure. It uproots the very foundation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), being eternally free from everything—cool and smokeless.
“Śāriputra! To state the essentials:
my Dharma completely destroys all conceptual thoughts, all views, all fetters, and all forms of overweening pride.”
One does not dwell upon any objects of recollection, and severs all various forms of speech.

Within this Dharma, there is neither permanence nor impermanence; neither suffering nor pleasure; neither defilement nor purity; neither annihilation nor eternity; neither self nor sentient being; neither person nor life-principle; neither a vital soul, nor arising, nor ceasing.
Why is this? Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata has attained nothing regarding phenomena and has extinguished nothing, it is called nirvāṇa; nor does he perceive anyone who attains nirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra! The Buddha does not think of nirvāṇa, nor does he take nirvāṇa as an object of thought, nor does he crave or cling to nirvāṇa.

Therefore, you should know that this is the foremost marvel and rarity: namely, that the Tathāgata causes people to believe and understand that all dharmas are without arising and without cessation, without marks and unconditioned; this is doubly rare.”
**Chapter 2: Mindfulness of the Buddha (Part One)** At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, within this Dharma, who is considered an evil friend?”
"What is meant by a 'good spiritual friend'?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If there is a bhikṣu who instructs another bhikṣu:"

“Monks! You should practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of generosity, and mindfulness of the devas. Monks!”
You should contemplate the body and grasp its characteristics, namely, its impurity.
You should contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being entirely impermanent, and contemplate all phenomena as empty and devoid of self.
"Monks! You should take up the sign of the object and bind the mind to that object, focusing single-mindedly on the sign of emptiness and delighting in wholesome qualities.

You should take up the sign of unwholesome qualities; having taken up the sign of unwholesome qualities, you should practice with mindfulness and reflection in order to abandon them—namely, by contemplating the sign of impurity in order to abandon sensual desire."
To sever hatred, one contemplates the aspect of loving-kindness;
to sever delusion, one contemplates the dharma of dependent origination.
Constantly mindful of pure precepts, one deeply grasps the mark of emptiness; with diligent application of vigor, one seeks the four dhyānas and strives single-mindedly for the Way.
One contemplates unwholesome phenomena as all being decay and affliction, and contemplates wholesome phenomena as the ultimate peace and security, practicing the Way with a single mind.

Having discerned and clearly contemplated wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, and having precisely grasped their characteristics, one contemplates only the peace, security, and quiescence of Nirvana, and cherishes only the ultimate purity of Nirvana.
Teaching in such a manner is called false teaching; that which is claimed to be the true teaching is in fact a false teaching.
Śāriputra, one who teaches in this way is called a bad friend (pāpamitra).
Such a person is said to slander me and assist non-Buddhists;
they also preach the teachings of false paths to others. Śāriputra!
For such evil persons, I do not permit even a single drink of water to be accepted for their own sustenance;
I speak of the teacher, not of the recipient. Śāriputra!
Within my Dharma, there are many such teachings of overweening pride. Śāriputra,

if a recipient of these teachings has been ordained for five years and cannot entirely relinquish such instructions, yet exerts himself with diligent effort within these teachings, he should not fail to go and consult those bhikṣus who have personally realized non-existence.

I say that although such a person may have [observed] the precepts for five years, they are still called one of wrong views who mingles with the teachings of external paths and follows the instructions of Māra.

"Śāriputra, if there is a bhikṣu who, having received these instructions, upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness and non-apprehension immediately realizes for himself: 'All that I previously accepted was wrong view,' and who thus has no doubt and no regret regarding the Dharma of emptiness and non-apprehension, penetrating it deeply and thoroughly, and no longer relying on any view of self or view of a person."
"Śāriputra! I say that such a person is called one who has attained pure brahmacarya. Śāriputra!"

If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes such patience of non-apprehension, although he has not yet attained nirvana without remainder in the present, I prophesy that this person shall be present at the first assembly during the time of Maitreya Buddha.
At that time, Maitreya Buddha will joyfully proclaim three times:
"This person has been able to achieve the patience of non-apprehension within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha. Śāriputra!
"If either a householder or one who has left the home life accomplishes this patience, I prophesy that such a person will certainly attain nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!

If there are those who, having received such instruction, are immediately startled and terrified upon hearing the Dharma of emptiness and non-attainment, these people are to be pitied; they have no savior and no refuge, and will go straight to hell."
Why is this? Śāriputra, those who are startled,
doubtful, or fearful within the Buddha’s teaching will be fully possessed by the evil realms.
Why is this? I have always said that those who hold to attainment belong to the realm of the evil paths.
For what reason?

"Śāriputra! The Dharma attained by the Buddha is without differentiation. If there were any distinction between what is 'this' and what is 'not this,' then there would be something attained. Śāriputra!"

It would be better for a person to commit the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution than to establish views of a self, a sentient being, a person, a life-span, a soul, or views regarding the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.
They are greedily attached to the observance of precepts and cling to views regarding the observance of precepts;
they are greedily attached to meditative concentration and cling to views regarding meditative concentration.
Relying on the notion of a Buddha, they conceive the notion of a Dharma, and through their deliberations concerning the Sangha, they establish the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Why is this? Within the Buddha-dharma, one who has established the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) does not belong to the number of the Saṃgha, Śāriputra!
The community of the Buddha’s disciples is free from conceptual differentiation. Śāriputra,
among the Buddha’s disciples there are none who are unwholesome, none who have broken the precepts, none who have broken their views, and none who have broken their dignified conduct.
“Śāriputra! What constitutes evil and unwholesome?
To be excluded from the count of the Saṃgha within the assembly of the Buddha is called evil and unwholesome.”

This refers to the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) which, when conjoined with various conditions, lack any real entity and consist merely of conceptual construction (vikalpa). Because of this conceptual construction, one imagines that there is something to be attained. All the verbal expressions, the continuous succession of mind and mental states, and even the wholesome or unwholesome dharmas of such a person are termed "evil and unwholesome" within the Noble Dharma.
Why is this? Śāriputra, wherever there is a state of pleasure, there must necessarily be suffering; the Dharma of the Tathāgata extinguishes both this suffering and pleasure.

“Śāriputra! That which is attained by the Tathāgata is herein without desire and without non-desire; it is without pleasure and without suffering; it is without thought, without perception, and without cultivation, even to the point of being without the perception of emptiness.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
if one reckons the perception of emptiness as the perception of a self or the perception of a sentient being, that is the perception of permanence or the perception of annihilation.
Why is this? Śāriputra, wherever there is conceptualization, various perceptions arise; all of these fall into error.
“Śāriputra! ‘Emptiness’ is named non-conceptualization; this is called emptiness. The conceptualization of emptiness is also empty; this is called emptiness. Śāriputra!”
In emptiness there is neither good nor evil, and even the notion of emptiness does not exist; therefore it is called "emptiness.
Śāriputra, all conditioned phenomena can be known and understood, but emptiness cannot be known and cannot be understood, nor can it be conceptualized; therefore it is called "emptiness."
Śāriputra! Emptiness is not attained through recollection. Why is this?
Because it is empty and without conceptualization, it is therefore called "empty.
Śāriputra, for what reason is it said that one practices the practice of emptiness?
Not to dwell upon any perceptions, even to the point of not dwelling upon the perception of emptiness itself—this is called the practice of emptiness.
"Śāriputra, 'perception' refers to anything from the mind having an object of thought; that which has no object of thought is called non-perception."
Because it is free from all perceptions, it is called "non-perception. Whatever perceptions one grasps are all false views.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Within the noble Dharma, even to conceive that one has attained nirvāṇa is to fall into false views; how much more so regarding verbal expression, and how much more so regarding the speaker?
Thus, by what means can this dharma of emptiness be expressed?
“Śāriputra! For what reason do the Buddhas say that all verbal expressions are termed ‘erroneous’?

Those who cannot penetrate all dharmas are entirely shrouded by verbal expression; therefore, the Tathāgata knows that all verbal expressions are erroneous, for even the slightest speech fails to accord with reality.”
“Śāriputra! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without conceptualization and without mentation. Why is this?
The Tathāgata does not apprehend the essential nature of dharmas, nor does he apprehend mindfulness.
"Śāriputra, for what reason does the Tathāgata speak of the foundations of mindfulness?"

Śāriputra! The Sūtra says that if a person attains the four foundations of mindfulness, it is impossible for that person to attain the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, or to attain a self-body, a self, or a person.
Because they demonstrate that the specific characteristics of phenomena are empty, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught.
As for the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness, it is without intrinsic nature, without location, without mindfulness, without speech, and without attachment.
If the very nature of mindfulness does not exist, how much less so the foundations of mindfulness?
Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of them by the name "foundations of mindfulness. Śāriputra!

If all phenomena possessed a determinate intrinsic nature even as small as one-hundredth part of a split hair, then the Buddhas would not appear in the world, nor would they ever teach that the nature of all phenomena is emptiness.
Śāriputra! All dharmas are truly empty and without intrinsic nature; they have but one characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless.
The Tathāgata perceives this completely, and for this reason, the Tathāgata speaks of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

“Śāriputra! The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are called ‘no place and no non-place,’ ‘no mindfulness and no activity of mindfulness,’ ‘no perception and no discrimination,’ ‘no mind and no mental activity,’ ‘no volition and no activity of volition,’ and ‘no phenomena and no characteristics of phenomena. All are without conjunction or dispersion; therefore, the noble ones (ārya) are called ‘those without discrimination. This is what is meant by the foundations of mindfulness.”
The Tathāgata speaks of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) for this reason: they are called foundations of mindfulness because they accord with non-existence;
they are called foundations of mindfulness because they accord with the recollection of the Buddha. "Śāriputra!..."
What is called "recollection of the Buddha"?
Seeing that there is nothing whatsoever is called recollection of the Buddha, Śāriputra.
The Buddhas are immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable; for this reason, to see that nothing exists is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
True name is non-discrimination, and the Buddhas are non-discriminative; therefore, it is said that mindfulness of non-discrimination is itself mindfulness of the Buddha.
Furthermore, seeing the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmas*) is called seeing the Buddha.
What is meant by the "true mark of all phenomena"?
It refers to the ultimate emptiness and non-existence of all phenomena; one should recollect the Buddha by means of these phenomena that are ultimately empty and non-existent.
Furthermore, within such a Dharma, even the slightest thought cannot be apprehended; this is called "recollection of the Buddha. Śāriputra!
This recollection of the Buddha cuts off the path of speech; it transcends all thoughts and is beyond being an object of recollection—this is called "recollection of the Buddha."
“Śāriputra! All thoughts are of the nature of quiescence; to accord with this Dharma is what is called the cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha.
One should not mindfully recollect the Buddha by means of form.”

Why is this? To recollect form by grasping its marks and craving its flavor constitutes consciousness; to be without form, without color, without objects, and without intrinsic nature—this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
"Therefore, you should know that to be without discrimination, without grasping, and without relinquishing is the true recollection of the Buddha.
**Chapter Three: Recollection of the Dharma (Part One)** At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In what way, World-Honored One, does one who teaches this Dharma to others become an evil friend? And in what way,
World-Honored One,
does one who teaches this Dharma to others become a virtuous friend?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If there is a bhikṣu who instructs another bhikṣu, saying: 'Bhikṣu!'"

You should now know that the act of mindfulness of the Buddha is empty; that which is the object of mindfulness is not to be mindfully grasped, for both the object you mindfully contemplate and the mindfulness itself are empty.
This emptiness of intrinsic nature can sever the perception of form and can sever the perception of grasping.
At that time, this person does not attain the state of non-conception, much less [retain] thought.

At that time, this person is entirely without anything, quiescent and devoid of intrinsic nature; they do not accumulate various conceptions and extinguish all dharmas—this is called the cultivation of mindfulness of the Buddha.

To recollect the Buddha means to shatter all wholesome and unwholesome discursive thoughts; to be without discursive thought or sustained contemplation, tranquil and free from ideation—this is called recollecting the Buddha. Why is this so?
One should not recollect the Buddhas through applied and sustained thought; that which is without applied or sustained thought is called pure mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within this mindfulness, there is not even the subtlest activity of mind or mental volition, let alone the activities of body or speech.

Furthermore, one who recollects the Buddha is free from all conceptualizations; these conceptualizations do not abide in the mind. There is no discrimination, no names, and no obstructions; there is neither desire nor attainment, and no arising of applied or sustained thought.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
all conceptualizations that arise according to what one thinks are all false views.
“Śāriputra! To accord with non-existence, without applied thought or sustained thought, without arising or ceasing—to penetrate this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within such mindfulness, there is no greed and no attachment; there is no opposition and no compliance; there is no name and no conceptualization.”

Śāriputra! To be without thought and without speech is what is called mindfulness of the Buddha; herein there is not even the slightest subtle thought, let alone coarse actions of body, speech, or mind.

To be without the spheres of body, speech, and mind; without grasping or rejecting; without contention or dispute; without thought or discrimination; empty, quiescent, and devoid of intrinsic nature; and to extinguish all discursive examination and investigation—this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.

“Śāriputra! If a person accomplishes such mindfulness, they can, according to their wish, overturn the earth of the four continents, and they can also subdue hundreds of thousands of billions of Māras; how much more so the wretched ignorance that arises from deceptive conditions and possesses no determinate characteristics?”

This Dharma is thus: it is without conceptualization and without discursive proliferation, without arising and without cessation, ineffable and beyond discrimination, without darkness and without light; it cannot be fathomed by Māra or the followers of Māra. Yet, for the sake of providing instruction through conventional speech, he says this:
"When you recollect the Buddha, do not grasp at small notions, do not give rise to discursive proliferation, and do not engage in discrimination."

Why is this? Because these dharmas are all empty, devoid of intrinsic nature, and inconceivable; they have but one characteristic, which is the so-called "characteristicless. This is called the true mindfulness of the Buddha—namely, that which is without arising and without cessation, without characteristics and unconditioned.

Why is this? The Tathāgata is not designated as form, nor as perception, nor as thought, nor as discrimination; he is neither contrary nor compliant, neither grasping nor relinquishing, neither concentration nor wisdom, and neither clarity nor ignorance.
The Tathāgata is ineffable, inconceivable, and signless; you should now take no pleasure in grasping at signs, nor take pleasure in conceptual proliferation.
Regarding all phenomena, the Buddha is without attachment and immeasurable, seeing no phenomenon whatsoever that can be grasped or measured.
"If even such a person cannot attain it regarding the Buddha, how much less so regarding mindfulness?
"Śāriputra, one who teaches in this way is called a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra)."
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no fixed determination that someone is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or a bad friend (*pāpamitra*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if there is a bhikṣu who instructs another bhikṣu:"
“Bhikṣu! You should analytically observe all dharmas, yet you must not even conceive of the characteristics of dharmas.

When this bhikṣu thus cultivates a mind free from attachment, he is able to penetrate the single characteristic of all dharmas, which is called “characteristiclessness. Such a person does not even give rise to the notion of dharmas, much less the notions of self or person.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Can one who dwells on the perception of dharmas extinguish all dharmas?
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
“Just as a tree without roots— could it have branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and seeds? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Thus it is, Śāriputra!
If a person does not apprehend the root of all dharmas, can that person give rise to the conceptualization of dharmas?
“No, [World-Honored One].”
“World-Honored One!
Śāriputra, if a person does not attain the non-conception of dharmas, can that person extinguish all dharmas?”
"No, World-Honored One!
This person does not attain dharmas, does not attain the characteristics of dharmas, and does not attain cessation; nor do they discriminate between non-arising and non-cessation."
At that time, this person neither arises nor ceases, and thus cannot be called one who has attained nirvāṇa;
yet, they likewise cannot be called one who has not attained nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!
One who teaches in this manner is called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*);
yet, within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is neither spiritual friend nor evil friend.
"Śāriputra!..."
If a person accomplishes such characteristics, they are rare in the world; because they attain the non-perverted, true vision, this constitutes right view.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Right view is called right action, right conduct, the right path, and right understanding.
Because it is free from inversion and perceives things as they truly are, the Tathāgata calls it right view.
Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who, being free from inversion, contemplate according to reality, they possess right view.
If they give rise to the notion of a self, the notion of a person, or the notion of a sentient being, you should know that such persons are all practicing erroneously.

“Śāriputra! The Buddha and his disciples do not speak of a self, do not speak of a person, do not speak of a sentient being, do not speak of a life-span, and do not speak of annihilation or permanence; for this reason, the Buddha and his disciples are said to possess right view.”
Why is this? Because right observation is non-perverted. "Śāriputra!
No ordinary person whatsoever is able to enter into this matter. Why is this?

Because all ordinary persons entirely lack right view; they may possess a compliance with right view that attains the patient acceptance of conformity (anulomikī kṣānti), yet they cannot [realize it] as it truly is, Śāriputra!
This is called the distinction between right view and wrong view.
Because one sees things as they truly are, it is called right view;
seeing the causes of worldly pleasure and the increase of wealth and profit as being correct is worldly right view, all of which is deceptive and does not exempt one from birth and death.
Śāriputra! When the Buddha speaks of "right view in the world," he is speaking of the dharma for those who are indolent and inferior;
the noble ones do not form such thoughts as, "This is right view" or "This is wrong view."
Why is this so? Because all views arise from false conditions. Śāriputra!
If one forms the thought,
"This is right view," that person is actually possessed of wrong view.

Śāriputra! Within the noble Dharma, one must uproot and sever the very foundation of all views and completely cut off all paths of verbal expression; just as a hand moving through space encounters no obstruction, so too should it be with all the dharmas of a śramaṇa.
4. Chapter on Mindfulness of the Sangha (Part One). Chapter Four: Mindfulness of the Sangha. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, what constitutes the Noble Assembly?”

“Śāriputra! If there is anyone who can have faith in, understand, and penetrate that all dharmas are without birth and without cessation, without arising and without marks, and who achieves such patience (kṣānti), they do not even attain a self, let alone the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, or anāgāmin.”
How much less could one attain arhatship?
How much less could one attain the Dharma?
How much less could one obtain sons or daughters?
How much less could they attain the Way?
How much less could they attain such matters as these?
They are called the Noble Assembly, yet even this cannot be attained.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are few sentient beings who are able to have faith and understanding in the dharma that is unborn, unceasing, and signless. Those who are able to have faith and understanding in the dharma that is unborn, unceasing, and signless possess minds free from inversion; they understand through mutual correspondence, and by being in harmony with the Dharma, they do not undergo further existence. They know that all worlds arise merely from false conditions."
Such a person no longer dwells in this body; for these reasons, they are called the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*).

Such a person cannot even be apprehended within these words and expressions, for all names and signs are merely a collection of signless and non-conceptual phenomena. This is called the Jewel of the Saṃgha, and it is worthy of receiving offerings.
Because they have attained the non-perverted, true meaning, this person uses such skillful means to recollect the Saṅgha, yet even this matter is empty. Śāriputra,
one who teaches in this way is called a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
“Śāriputra! The severing of all paths of speech is called the Noble Assembly. Why is this?

Within the Noble Dharma, although one speaks of the true meaning by means of language, such language itself is unattainable; therefore, one should know that the cessation of all language is called the Noble Assembly.
“Śāriputra! Suppose someone were to say:
‘If within this there is no speech and no fixed [dharma], how can it be called the Saṃgha?’”
"Śāriputra! In this regard, I have answered thus:

'The Sangha is called that which demonstrates things as they truly are; yet this thing is determined to be unobtainable. They are all of one training, one forbearance, and one flavor. This matter is also spoken of by way of conventional language, not in the ultimate sense.'"
"In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no fixed, real entity called the 'Dharma of the Sangha' that is eternal and indestructible.
If a noble one were to say that such a dharma exists, that would constitute a defilement.

Why is this? Because if a person makes such discriminations as "this is male," "this is female," "this is a deva," "this is a nāga," "this is a yakṣa," "this is a gandharva," "this is a kumbhāṇḍa," "this is dharma," or "this is adharma."
Having made such distinctions, one encounters various phenomena; because of encountering these various phenomena, one speaks thus:
"This is sitting, this is lying down, this is walking, and this is standing."

Because the Noble One has attained the true reality of all phenomena (dharmas), he does not discriminate between male and female, deva and nāga, nor even between what is dharma and what is non-dharma.
Because they do not engage in conceptual discrimination, they do not apprehend various phenomena.
Since they do not apprehend various phenomena, could they say, "This is sitting," "This is lying down," "This is walking," or "This is standing"?
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
If someone were to say, "This is a man, this is a woman; this is a deva, this is a nāga," and so on, up to "this is Dharma, this is non-Dharma," would what that person says not be false?
"It is false, World-Honored One! "Śāriputra!
If one does not enter into this falsehood, they are called the noble assembly.
Because they are free from inversion, they are called the noble assembly, Śāriputra!
All that is unwholesome, all that is knowable, and all that is attainable—all such unwholesome dharmas whatsoever—have name and appearance as their basis.

Within this Dharma of the noble ones, all names and signs are severed; furthermore, one does not dwell upon names and signs nor grasp at them. How, then, could one say "this is a noble one" or "this is the assembly"?
The severing of all names and signs is what is called the "assembly of noble ones."

If there were any dharma-position that could be broken or severed, then within the Dharma of the noble ones (ārya), which is nameless, signless, and beyond speech, all discourse would be severed, and there would be no joining or dispersing. To say that there is no Sangha would be to destroy the community of the noble ones, yet even this is not possible.

Because one falsely conceptualizes names and marks, one clings to various false views; due to these false views, one further undergoes future births, and through attachment to these views, the five aggregates arise.
Śāriputra! The five aggregates are all false attachments; these are called the evil paths and are called wrong views.

Among the assembly of noble ones, such things do not exist; they merely know that because of false conditions, one arises within the triple world. Because they know this matter, they are called the assembly of noble ones.
“Śāriputra, whatever views there may be, none of them can be found among the noble assembly; that is to say:”

The view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a person, the view of a male, the view of a female, the view of a deva, the view of a hell-being, the view of an animal, the view of a hungry ghost; the view of the aggregates, the bases, and the elements; the view of the sound of a conch, the sound of a drum, the sound of the earth, the sounds of water, fire, and wind; the view of the sound of observing precepts, the view of the sound of violating precepts; the view of the sound of the right path, the view of the sound of the wrong path; the views of the sounds of defilement and purity, the sounds of dhyāna, samādhi, and the eightfold noble path; the views of the sounds of the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; the view of the sound of liberation, the view of the sound of attaining the fruits, the view of the sound of the Buddha, the view of the sound of the Dharma, the view of the sound of the Saṅgha, the view of the sound of cessation, and the view of the sound of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! This is called the view of false sounds and so forth.

As for the assembly of noble ones (ārya), they do not find such views within the ultimate truth (paramārtha). They penetrate all various sounds as having a single characteristic—namely, the characteristicless (animitta)—and because they have accomplished the patience regarding the non-perverted dharma (aviparīta-dharma-kṣānti) without conflict or contention, they are called the noble assembly.
“Śāriputra! This non-perverted patience of dharmas is precisely signlessness (*animitta*).
Because it is signless, there is no grasping and no abandoning; no opposition and no compliance; no arising and no ceasing. Within this, one naturally returns to extinction.”
There is no cultivation and no destruction, no arising and no attainment; because one does not discriminate between this and that, the mind is always detached. Why is this so?

Within this patience (*kṣānti*), there is no hither shore and no further shore, no discrimination and no non-discrimination. To penetrate the signless (*animitta*) and accomplish this patience is called the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*); because it breaks through the combination [of extremes], it is called the Noble Assembly.
“Śāriputra! In another sūtra I have said:
‘If a person sees the Dharma, that is seeing me; the Tathāgata is neither the Dharma nor non-Dharma.’”
Why is this? Because the foolish Devadatta and all the non-Buddhists all perceive the Buddha by means of his physical body (*rūpakāya*). Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the physical body, nor should he be seen by means of his voice.
Śāriputra, if a person sees the Buddha by means of the physical body, they are far removed from the Buddha.
Why is this? One does not say that the Buddha is seen through his physical form; rather, one says that the Buddha is seen [through the Dharma]. Śāriputra!
If a person can see that all phenomena are signless—without name, without contact, without recollection, without thought, without arising, without ceasing, and without conceptual proliferation;

if they do not dwell upon any phenomena, do not dwell upon nirvāṇa, do not take nirvāṇa as an object of thought, and do not crave nirvāṇa, but have faith and understanding that all phenomena are of a single characteristic, namely, signlessness.
Śāriputra! This is called truly seeing the Buddha.
That is to say, all dharmas are without seeking, without conceptual proliferation, and without arising; within this state, one neither recollects nor discriminates—this is called seeing the Buddha.
If there is a person who, within this Dharma, is without recollection or conceptualization, without grasping or rejecting, without attachment or aversion, and without thought or the karma of thought;

who does not crave verbal expression, knowing that dharmas are merely provisional names and that all are non-existent; who has severed the path of speech, being without differentiation and without frivolous proliferation—this is called one who practices the non-arising and non-conceptualizing way, and among the world, such a person is termed a member of the Noble Assembly.
“Śāriputra! By seeing what dharma is one said to ‘see the Buddha’?
It is that which is without conceptualization, without discrimination, without proliferation, and does not grasp at any dharma.”

Whether by way of the gate of emptiness, the gate of cessation, or the gate of detachment, one does not conceive of seeing nor obtain seeing; even this matter is unobtainable—namely, what is called "name. Even this locus is unobtainable—namely, what is called "nirvāṇa."
For what reason? Śāriputra,
since I do not even conceive of nirvāṇa, how could I say that you should conceive of nirvāṇa or that you should attain nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra! If there were anyone who had attained nirvāṇa, that person would not have gone forth following the Tathāgata, but would have gone forth following the six teachers. Śāriputra!
You should know that such a person is a thief of the Dharma who has entered into my teaching;
you should know that such a person defiles and brings disgrace upon my Dharma;
you should know that such a person is a great thief, like a great thief within a large city.
Why is this? Such deluded people do not even attain nirvana, let alone [the states of] self or person. Śāriputra!
Such deluded people I ward off with my hand; they are not my disciples, they do not enter the ranks of the assembly, and I am not their teacher. Śāriputra!

If one knows that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, without thought and without conceptualization, and attains this patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), such a person does not even attain nirvāṇa—how much less so, then, for a self or a person?
"Śāriputra! The Buddha has taught that such is called 'seeing the Dharma'; to be able to see this matter is called 'seeing the Buddha. Śāriputra!"
What is meant by "Buddha"?
The suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is neither different nor destructible; this is called the Tathāgata.
If a person has no doubt or regret regarding these phenomena, they are called the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*).

“Śāriputra, in a past age there was a foolish man who did not recognize monkeys. Entering a great forest, he saw a troop of monkeys gathered together in one place. Having previously heard that there were gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he immediately claimed they were the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.”
He immediately emerged from the forest and returned to his native village, where, amidst a great multitude of people, he spoke these words:
"Have you all ever seen the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?
The crowd replied:
"I have never seen it before.
He immediately replied,
"I have already seen it."
"Do you wish to see it?
They all replied,
"We wish to see it."
He then led the great assembly to that grove and pointed out the troop of monkeys, saying:
"All of you, observe these gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Everyone said:
"This is not a Trāyastriṃśa deva; this is a monkey who delights in dwelling within the forest.
Because you are deluded and inverted, you do not recognize the monkey, nor do you recognize the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven."
“Śāriputra! This person will vainly lead a great multitude to that forest.
It is even so, Śāriputra!”
In future ages, there will be bhikṣus who go to the homes of laypeople and say:
"Do you wish to see the Buddha and the noble Saṃgha? Do you wish to hear the Buddha’s Dharma?
Among them, those laypeople who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma will all say:
"I wish to see and hear the Buddha-dharma.

Śāriputra, among them there are laypeople who, craving the pleasure of speech, enter monasteries; and there are bhikṣus who delight in talk, are able to recite various sutras, rely upon speech, and take pleasure in literary embellishment. These śramaṇas preach to them in accordance with their inclinations, claiming it is the true path, yet they merely serve to swell the numbers of the assembly like cowherds.
They take pleasure only in reciting scriptures but do not enter the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*);
they delight only in pleasing others and prize fame and profit; they are skillful in worldly affairs but preach the Dharma without purity;

they are only able to speak with eloquence and follow the paths of the world, lacking majestic virtue and destroying the causes for *nirvāṇa*. Having abandoned holy silence, they take no pleasure in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*); day and night they constantly enjoy talk and dispute. Reclining upon thick bedding and furs, they lack even a single thought of compliance with meditative concentration, let alone being able to attain the fruits of a *śramaṇa*.

This person sleeps constantly with a mind associated with worldly concerns; during the first and last watches of the night, they do not cultivate compliant patience and take pleasure in inferior dharmas. Such a person also receives much provision of clothing, food, and drink.

Why is this? Because such people are constantly influenced by evil Māras who delight in shallow and superficial discourse; they are unable to diligently study the primary truth, nor can they recite or uphold the most profound sutras. Upon hearing them, they are struck with alarm and fear, abandoning the pure essence to seize only the dregs.
Śāriputra, there are certain ordinary worldlings who, seeing the acquisition of gain and offerings, give rise to a mind of greedy attachment and think to themselves:
"We, too, should practice this discourse. Śāriputra!
Such a person has abandoned the unsurpassed jewel of the Dharma and fallen into false views; they are a *caṇḍāla* among śramaṇas.

When laypeople go to them, such evil persons preach the Dharma for them, praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha for the sake of gain and sustenance. Seeking only to sustain their lives, they act as slaves to wealth, greedily craving food and clothing, and praise what they themselves enjoy, saying:
"If one practices giving, one will be reborn in the heavens."
Within the Buddha-dharma, they treat giving as an inferior practice, yet they praise it as supreme, saying:
"By the causes and conditions of great giving, one attains birth in the heavens."

They do not understand speech nor grasp its underlying meaning; they know only how to enter into shallow and inferior teachings, becoming greedily attached to the notions of self and person, and thus abandoning the ultimate truth.

“Śāriputra! When the Dharma is taught in this way, there may be those who, having conceived faith, leave the household life, yet associate with evil people and are unable to diligently seek the foremost, profound meaning.”

Those who perceive something as obtainable speak of a self, a person, a life-span, and a soul; they conceptualize and discriminate regarding dharmas that do not exist, engaging in their own debates within the Abhidharma and Sūtras, sometimes speaking of annihilationism or eternalism, sometimes of action, and sometimes of non-action.
“Śāriputra! At that time, my Dharma will abound with the teachings of non-Buddhists, causing the right view of sentient beings to be destroyed.
It is thus, Śāriputra!”
"By these causes and conditions, my pure Dharma will gradually perish and come to an end. Śāriputra!
This Bodhi which I have attained after enduring various sufferings and afflictions throughout the long course of saṃsāra will be destroyed at that time by such evil people."

Śāriputra! If there are bhikṣus who cannot relinquish these views of apprehending something, the view of a self, and the view of a person; who do not understand that the Tathāgata’s teachings were spoken according to what was appropriate for the occasion; and who assert with certainty that there is a self, a person, and dharmas.
For such a person, I do not permit even the acceptance of a single drink of water.

However, if at some time this person hears the Dharma of emptiness and their faith becomes pure without alarm or doubt, they should immediately lead others to enter the meaning of the true nature (*dharmatā*), and should then leave the household life to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If a person does not abandon such views, they are called a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).
“Śāriputra! I provisionally speak of a ‘self’ by means of worldly causes and conditions; it is not from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
If someone were to say:”
"I also speak of a self by means of worldly causes and conditions.
If a person can thoroughly penetrate the dharma that is without arising and without cessation, and without marks, such that it does not contradict what I have taught, they are my disciple.
Śāriputra! If someone were to say:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata, in accordance with worldly causes and conditions, speak of a 'person' within the dharma of non-self?"
The Tathāgata should not intentionally utter untruths for the sake of the world;
furthermore, since many sūtras speak of the existence of persons, what the Buddha has taught ought not to be false.
"Śāriputra! You should answer that person:

'The Buddha has taught that all dharmas are empty, without a master, and without intrinsic nature; they are merely illusory and not the ultimate truth (paramārtha). It is not on account of the ultimate truth that the Tathāgata speaks of a self or a person.'"
“The speech of the Sage is free from all attachment; there is no person without wisdom who is equal to the Buddha, nor is there anyone who surpasses him.
Śāriputra, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; with this wisdom he knows the minds of sentient beings. How could there ever be anyone equal to the Buddha?”
The Buddha is a great dragon and the king of the great Dharma;
one should not challenge him by saying, "The Buddha says there is a person.
All the world constantly disputes with me, yet I never dispute with the world.

“Śāriputra! Those who speak of a self are truly to be pitied; herein there is neither dharma nor a self. Many sentient beings do not understand the Tathāgata’s teachings given according to their needs, and by opposing the Jewel of the Dharma, they mostly fall into the evil destinies.”
Śāriputra! I know wrong views, yet I do not engage in wrong views; one who is able to know wrong views is precisely one who possesses right view. Śāriputra!
"Wrong view never transforms into right view;
one who views does not know viewing. Śāriputra!"

The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is difficult for all the world to believe; among all the devas and the entire world, I am the one most worthy of trust, not unworthy of trust.
Śāriputra! The Dharma I teach is for the sake of reaching the other shore, yet within it there is no one who reaches the other shore;
the Dharma I teach is for the sake of exhausting all conditioned formations, yet within it there is no one who exhausts all conditioned formations.
The Dharma I teach is for the sake of quiescence, yet within it there is no one who is quiescent;
the Dharma I teach is for the sake of nirvāṇa, yet within it there is no one who attains nirvāṇa;
the Dharma I teach is for the sake of liberation, yet within it there is no one who is liberated.
The Dharma I teach is for the sake of those who possess wisdom, yet within it there are no such wise ones;
the Dharma I teach is for the sake of purifying defilements, yet within it there are no such things as purity or defilement.
Śāriputra! When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for devas, there are no devas;
when he preaches the Dharma for humans, there are no humans.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, yet there are no sentient beings. Śāriputra,
when the Tathāgata speaks of ignorance and liberation, therein is neither ignorance nor liberation.
I say that when one recollects the Buddha, the Buddha is not to be recollected;
I say that when one practices emptiness, emptiness is neither to be practiced nor to be recollected. Śāriputra!
These are called the chapters and phrases of the sūtra-dharma spoken by the Tathāgata.

Within them, there is no speaker; yet wicked people who obtain these chapters and phrases will preach them to others, taking me as their teacher. Though they lack the merit of the Tathāgata’s noble assembly, they consider themselves to be among the ranks of the Saṃgha.
Śāriputra! For example, a troop of monkeys does not resemble the Trāyastriṃśa devas;
likewise, these many evil people do not resemble my noble assembly.
Śāriputra! These evil persons merely call themselves śramaṇas by means of sounds and speech; they are like foolish people who, upon seeing a troop of monkeys, claim them to be the Trāyastriṃśa gods.

“Śāriputra! Among those who have left the household life, there are some who delight in posing difficult questions and encounter a virtuous teacher, who explains for them the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the severance of the path of language, the absence of arising and passing away, and the penetration of signlessness (*animitta*).”

Those who, upon hearing such a Dharma that is without arising, without cessation, and without marks, do not feel startled or afraid, should be known as people who have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past; they are able to understand my Dharma and may be called the Noble Assembly.
Chapter Five: On Pure Precepts (Part One of Two). The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“A bhikṣu who has violated the precepts possesses ten arrows of affliction that are difficult to endure.”

If a bhikṣu is pierced by ten arrows of affliction, he will find no flavor in the Buddha’s Dharma; he will harbor hatred toward those who preach the Dharma and take no pleasure in associating with them.
What are these ten?
Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts does not give rise to a joyful mind when seeing the Saṃgha in harmony. Why is this?
When the *poṣadha* is performed in communal harmony, they will surely expel me.
This evil bhikṣu, knowing he has committed a transgression, constantly harbors anxiety and distress; he feels resentment and displeasure toward those who uphold the precepts.
“Śāriputra! This is called the first arrow of anxiety and distress for a precept-breaking bhikṣu; he will certainly fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”

A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is loathed by the community and no one desires to associate with him; he is like a vicious bull with sharp horns whom people abandon and keep at a distance. This evil bhikṣu, knowing himself to be at fault, constantly harbors anxiety and distress.
"Śāriputra! These are called the two arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu; he will certainly fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a precept-breaking bhikṣu encounters a community of bhikṣus, he knows himself to be unlike them; with a malicious mind, he abandons them, and because he harbors shame and humiliation, he cannot enter the assembly. Śāriputra!
This is called the three arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu, who will inevitably fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the poisonous and evil mind of a precept-breaking bhikṣu is so rampant that it cannot be transformed even by the disciplinary laws of non-Buddhists, let alone by the pure precepts.
Because of the causes and conditions of their broken precepts, people do not draw near them. Śāriputra!
These are called the four arrows of affliction for a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts; he will inevitably fall into the evil realms.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a precept-breaking bhikṣu who nourishes his own body with the wealth and property of others— I call such a person a bearer of a heavy burden. Why is this so?
The practitioner and the attainer are worthy of receiving offerings; a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is neither a practitioner nor an attainer.
Therefore, Śāriputra!

A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts shall, for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas, cut off pieces of his own flesh to repay the donor; if he is born into the bodies of animals, he will constantly bear heavy burdens.

Why is this? Suppose a single hair were divided into a thousand billion parts; a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts cannot even digest the offering of one such part, much less can he digest the clothing, food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites provided by others.

Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts, even though he wears the sacred Dharma robes, should not take even a single step into a monastery; how much less should he receive so much as a sip of water, let alone a bed or a couch?
Why is this? Śāriputra, such evil persons are great thieves among gods and humans; all the world should keep them at a distance.
Śāriputra! Such a person who brings about ruin is an enemy.
The Tathāgata permits all those in the world to come to my presence; however, one who has broken the precepts is barred by the Tathāgata’s own hand and is not my disciple.
How much more so for one who dwells within my Dharma for even a single day?

Śāriputra, it is like a dead person, a dead snake, or a dead dog, which are most foul and putrid; when the pure devas wish to sport, they must not see them, and if they do see them, they keep their distance.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

A bhikṣu who violates the precepts is like those three corpses—foul-smelling, filthy, and impure; the wise keep their distance from him and do not engage in communal activities such as the poṣadha or the pravāraṇa with him.
Śāriputra! A precept-breaking bhikṣu is inauspicious within my Dharma; a precept-observing bhikṣu, upon seeing such a precept-breaker, immediately distances himself from him.
Why is this? Śāriputra, whatever object a precept-breaking bhikṣu touches with his hand or receives is like poison and evil to one who upholds the precepts. Śāriputra!

Even if three corpses were to fill the ground with their foul stench, I could move through them while maintaining the four modes of deportment; yet I cannot dwell for even a moment with this precept-breaking bhikṣu.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
This is considered base, lowly, and ignoble among śramaṇas.
They are the rotten and corrupt among śramaṇas;
they are the chaff among śramaṇas;
they are the defilement among śramaṇas.
They are a turbidity among śramaṇas;
they are a defilement among śramaṇas;
they are a crookedness among śramaṇas.
They are the coarsest among śramaṇas;
they are those among śramaṇas who have lost the Noble Path.
People such as these, having left the household life within my Dharma to seek the Way, incur a grave offense.
Śāriputra!

Such a person within my Dharma is a rebel, a thief of the Dharma, and a person of deceit and hypocrisy; seeking only to sustain their life while greedily coveting food and clothing, they are called a slave to worldly pleasures.
Śāriputra! Just as a eunuch is neither male nor female, so it is with a precept-breaking bhikṣu; he is called neither a layperson nor a renunciant, and after his life ends, he goes straight to hell.
Śāriputra! It is like the bat:

when it wishes to catch birds, it enters its hole and becomes a mouse; when it wishes to catch mice, it flies through the air and becomes a bird. Yet, in reality, it possesses none of the utility of a great bird; its body is foul and filthy, and it delights only in darkness.
Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts is also like this:

he neither participates in the poṣadha nor the pravāraṇa; he does not enter the service of kings, nor is he called a layman, nor is he called one who has left the home life. He is like the charred remains of a funeral pyre, no longer fit for use.
Thus it is, bhikṣu!

There is no aggregate of morality, no aggregate of concentration, no aggregate of wisdom, no aggregate of liberation, and no aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; there is only the possession of the aggregate of the breaking of pure morality.

They are unable to produce great, subtle, and wondrous sounds—the sound of precepts, the sound of concentration, the sound of wisdom, the sound of liberation, and the sound of the knowledge and vision of liberation—but instead produce the foul and evil sounds of violating the precepts, uttering such wicked cries in the company of those who share their evil ways.

They discuss only matters of clothing, food, drink, and bedding; they accept gifts of trees, flowers, and fruits; they act as servants to the noble; and they discourse on the auspiciousness or misfortune, safety or danger, and the various trivialities of worldly affairs with laughter—all such unwholesome speech. Constantly, day and night, they seek out defilements; such, O Bhikṣu, are these!
With impurity of bodily action, impurity of verbal action, and impurity of mental action, one shall fall into hell.
Śāriputra, such a precept-breaking bhikṣu delights in darkness; like a bat, he feels distress when hearing the preaching of the True Sūtras.
Why is this? Because they speak according to reality.

People of the world do not delight in speaking the truth but only take pleasure in what accords with their own wishes; likewise, such bhikṣus have impure minds toward those who preach the Dharma, and by committing further offenses, they increase their burden in hell.
"Śāriputra! These are called the five arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu; he will certainly fall into hell.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The precept-breaking bhikṣu is devoid of shame; his faculties are scattered and he has accomplished impurity. His physical, verbal, and mental actions lack pure deportment, and the robes he wears are entirely contrary to the Dharma. He delights in false speech and cannot guard his mouth; his mind constantly runs wild, defiled by filth and impurity.

Śāriputra! Suppose a new earthenware vessel were filled with excrement, urine, foul-smelling pus, and blood; later, after removing the impurities, sandalwood incense were placed inside, and then the sandalwood was removed—what kind of odor would such a vessel have?
“World-Honored One!
This new earthenware vessel was previously filled with excrement and urine; its foul odor is firmly adhered to it, such that there is only the stench and no fragrance of sandalwood.
“Śāriputra! [the Buddha said.]
People who have left the household life to study the Way with pure faith and the other faculties may encounter evil associates and follow their teachings.
Śāriputra, what constitutes an evil associate?

An evil associate is one who constantly delights in frivolous jesting and is flighty and shameless; their speech is distracted and they fail to restrain their sense faculties; their mind is not single-minded and they are as ignorant as a white sheep.

Those who associate with such evil associates lose the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; they even lose the joy of rebirth in the heavens, let alone the path to nirvana.

If one merely cultivates and accumulates the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, and associates with those who destroy the Dharma, that person will accomplish impure physical karma, impure verbal karma, and impure mental karma, as well as impure observance of the precepts; after death, they shall enter the evil destinies.
What are the evil destinies?
The evil destinies are known as the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.

Furthermore, there are other evil paths such as those of the *ayūla* worm, the *vāgalamukha* worm, the *bhūmiśuṣkā* worm, and the *śilīmukha* worm; such persons are often reborn among these various insects.

Śāriputra! Such a person follows evil associates; even if born among humans, they will suffer separation from parents, death, and loss; their kinsmen will decline and suffer distress, and their country will be destroyed.

Born into one of the eight difficult conditions, they abandon the eight states of happiness; they are full of desire, anger, and delusion, always fond of frivolous play, flighty and shameless, with distracted speech, unable to collect their minds.

Foolish as white sheep, they are ruined by greed, anger, and delusion; deaf, mute, blind, and with hands and feet withered and crippled, they associate with evil companions and are born in places where no Buddha dwells.
If one encounters the era of a Buddha, yet finds no joy in seeing him with the eyes, no joy in hearing the Dharma, and does not harmonize with the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples;
if one gives rise to such evil karma, being born among evil people and delighting in inferior dharmas, conceiving the notion of false views within right view,
and conceiving the notion of right view within false views— this is called inferior desire, inferior patience, and inferior wisdom.
"Śāriputra!
A person of inferior wisdom can never give rise to the thought of weariness with suffering, renunciation, cessation, the path, or nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!"
Having encountered evil associates, they undergo such various forms of decline, affliction, and suffering; such are their characteristics.

When these people hear these profound sūtras and teachings, they are startled, doubtful, and terrified as if falling into a deep pit, and thus they fall into the deep pit and trench of great transgressions.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
As it is said in the sūtras, a bhikṣu who violates the precepts incurs a grave and heavy offense.
For what reasons and conditions is one called "one who has broken the precepts"?
Because they have violated the precepts they undertook, they are difficult to instruct;
because their conduct lacks a constant standard, they are full of contradictions and opposition.
Constantly practicing greed and attachment, engaging in many mixed and impure actions;
practicing desire, anger, and delusion while delighting in various frivolous words—this is called breaking the precepts.
Furthermore, there are those who delight in many worldly affairs, delight in excessive recitation, and delight in excessive sleep.
Their speech is discordant and lacks sequential order;
their teaching is impure, as they are greedily attached to the notions of a self, a person, a life-span, and a living being; for these reasons, they are called wicked bhikṣus.
They do not know moderation in measure; they do not know the Dharma of the śramaṇas, nor the Dharma of the brāhmaṇas.
They delight in practicing medical arts and seeking profit through trade;
they delight in serving as envoys for states and defiling various households.
He delights in serving and performing labor for laypeople;
he offers various tree leaves, flowers, and fruits to them; he is fond of preaching the teachings of non-Buddhists to laypeople;
his mind is constantly detached from supramundane dharmas; and he received full ordination before reaching twenty years of age—these are matters concerning the reception of the precepts.
There are those who are incomplete, lacking in physical form; they are unfit for the Dharma, receiving rice, grain, money, silk, gold, and silver.
They do not comply with instructions and resist the commands of their teachers. They are unaware of themselves and unaware of others;
they cannot distinguish between the noble and the base, nor between superior and inferior grades. They delight in false speech and are greedily attached to the grasping of precepts. Their conduct...
Their minds are distracted and lack single-mindedness; their faces bear expressions of anger, and they are stingy, greedy, and faithless.
They do not recognize kindness or righteousness, harboring much covetousness, sloth, frivolity, doubt and regret, and resentment.
They conceal their evil deeds, delighting in self-assertion and obstinacy; they are envious, sycophantic, shameless, and lacking in remorse, being arrogant and heedless.
They are possessed of conceit, self-conceit, great conceit, and false conceit.

They delight in practicing deception and praising themselves; they employ many expedient means to open doors for gain and offerings, and they treat laypeople with contempt while feigning intimacy. By exploiting their influence, they acquire wealth to boast among the multitude, thereby destroying the categories of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Their minds lack settled faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; they do not believe in karmic retribution, valuing only immediate benefits; they claim there is no future life and harbor many doubts and regrets; their dispositions are shallow and weak, and they are constantly prone to alarm and fear.
Śāriputra! These are called wicked bhikṣus.

Such deluded people within my Dharma are like excrement, urine, foul odors, and impurities. Because these individuals have accomplished deeds of body, speech, and mind that are not pure, after their lives end, they will fall into evil realms and enter the great hells.
Thus it is, bhikṣu!
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and their assemblies of disciples always remain far removed from such things; other seekers of the Way who strive for nirvāṇa likewise keep themselves at a distance.
Śāriputra! It is as if, for example, sandalwood were placed in an impure vessel; it becomes identical to the impurity and can no longer be used.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!

If householders or renunciants associate with such a person and imitate their conduct, they too will soon break the precepts and become like them; their complexions will become haggard and their dignified deportment will be lost, and after the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the hells.
Śāriputra! Such evil persons are shunned by all the Tathāgatas and their assemblies of disciples, as well as by others who seek the Way and delight in nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! It is as if, for example, sandalwood placed in an impure vessel can no longer be used.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, just as those who are either householders or renunciants remain defiled even when they anoint their bodies,
so too it is with these wicked bhikṣus!

Although he sits among the assembly wearing the sacred robes of the Dharma, his appearance as a wicked bhikṣu still manifests; when bhikṣus of pure conduct see this impurity, they keep their distance and do not draw near.
When seeing others maintain detachment, his mind becomes resentful; by reason of this, he dies and enters hell.
Śāriputra, these are called the six arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu, and he will certainly fall into hell.

The Remainder of the Chapter on Pure Precepts:

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a precept-breaking bhikṣu hears such sūtras as these spoken by the Buddha, his mind is not pure, nor does he feel joy, faith, or delight; knowing himself to be at fault, he then suspects this sūtra, thinking:"
"Speak for our sake and not for others.
Why? Because we bhikṣus are present here for this purpose."

"Śāriputra! Regarding such a supreme, wondrous, and peerless Dharma, a precept-breaking bhikṣu will give rise to anger and resentment; his mind will harbor much lack of faith toward the one who preaches the Dharma. Upon hearing such a sutra spoken by the Buddha, he will oppose it and refuse to accept it, saying:
'This was not spoken by the Buddha; teach it to others.'"
Why is this? A bhikṣu who violates the precepts does not delight in cultivating the Path, whereas a bhikṣu who cultivates the Path does not contravene the Buddha’s words.
These are all evil dharmas of ignorance resulting from broken precepts; they consist of a mind that lacks faith and rebels against the Buddha’s words.
