In this way, a bhikṣu, though aware of his own transgressions, gives rise only to resentment, arrogance, perversity, and a mind of evil, heterodoxy, and conceit, thereby slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Śāriputra!
Following this, that bhikṣu hears these various sūtras and, being contrary to them, does not believe them; his mind fails to penetrate the unsurpassed bodhi, and he instructs others, saying:
"These were not spoken by the Buddha."
Śāriputra! The Buddha says that such a person slanders the Dharma.
Because they slander the Dharma, they are neither śramaṇas nor sons of the Śākya; they should be expelled.

Even if hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas were to manifest the three wheels of action for these bhikṣus, they could not cause them to awaken and attain the fruits of the Path. Why is this?

Śāriputra! Such evil persons create obstacles for themselves on the path within this Dharma; they no longer possess the potential for rebirth in the higher realms nor do they have faith. Merely fond of fine food and clothing, they greedily delight in worldly gain. I say that such people will certainly fall into hell.

“Śāriputra! I now tell you clearly and plainly: if a person opposes such a jewel of the Dharma, they shall never have a share in rebirth in a favorable realm; instead, they will always be born in an evil realm, forever blind and sightless.”

Śāriputra! These bhikṣus, their arrogance blazing fiercely, are unable to speak with certainty; they destroy my True Dharma, and the rest of the people, being unable to sustain themselves, follow and destroy my Dharma for the sake of gain and offerings.
Śāriputra! In this way, the Dharma-treasure will perish at that time. Why is this?
This Dharma-treasure is revered by all Buddhas alike, and it is likewise revered by *pratyekabuddhas*, *arhats*, and others.

At that time, monks who have broken the precepts, those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and monks who preach the Dharma indistinctly will all together treat my Dharma with contempt and distance themselves from it. They will harbor much greed and envy, focusing solely on seeking a livelihood; bound by jealousy, they will value wealth and profit. Always fond of litigation, they will create mutual enmity and resentment; lacking mutual respect and compliance, they will be devoid of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*). Their dispositions will be fickle and restless like monkeys; shifting their deportment, they will perform various evil deeds, falling away from the *śramaṇa* dharma and distancing themselves from the noble ones (*ārya*).

Śāriputra! Such evil persons conceal their flaws, possessing great desire and seeking much, sustaining themselves through wealth. Knowing their minds, Māra employs skillful means to cause discord among them, leading to their mutual destruction; thus the Sangha-treasure of one flavor is divided into five sects.
Once there are five schools, disputes arise, and they engage in mutual arguments of right and wrong, discussing each other's faults. Śāriputra!
Now, however, these bhikṣus teach one another and respect one another; with a single mind they practice together, remaining in accord with the Buddha’s words.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not exhort one another nor show mutual respect; seeing those who committed evil, they would fearfully abandon them, unable to instruct and admonish one another according to the Dharma.

At times, even though they possess extensive learning and profound wisdom, they still harbor arrogance and look down upon others; each establishes their own doctrines based on what they deem correct, taking no pleasure in meeting one another, let alone being able to accept instruction.
“Śāriputra! While the Tathāgata remains in the world, the Three Jewels are of one flavor; after my parinirvāṇa, they shall be divided into five schools. Śāriputra!”

Even now, the evil Māra remains hidden, assisting Devadatta in his attempt to destroy my Dharma and Saṃgha; yet, because the Tathāgata’s great wisdom is present in the world, this wicked Māra cannot accomplish such great evil.

In future ages, evil Māras will manifest in transformed bodies, assuming the form of śramaṇas and entering among the Saṃgha; they will propagate various heterodox doctrines, causing many sentient beings to fall into false views by preaching perverted teachings, such as those concerning Meru, Dhara, and Garuḍa.
The five categories of contentious matters are: matters that perish moment by moment, matters that exist in all things, matters of existence, matters of self, and matters of attainment.
At that time, the evil Māra spoke of such perverse attachments; such matters as these are not taught by the Buddhas or their disciples.
At that time, evil persons, deluded by Māra, each cling to their own views, asserting "I am right and they are wrong. Śāriputra!
Because the Tathāgata foresees such occurrences of the destruction of the Dharma in future ages, he preaches this profound sūtra to completely sever all the attachments held by evil Māras.

“Śāriputra! At that time, within Jambudvīpa, there will be many people of overweening pride who, having performed only minor acts of goodness, will immediately claim to have attained the Way; after their lives end, they shall fall into the evil realms.”

Why is this? Because such a person, throughout the long night, claims for themselves that they have attained the Way, and likewise proclaims to others that they have attained the Way; they presumptuously accept the offerings and services due to a Noble One. Such a person is a great evil thief among the devas, humans, and the world.
When such deluded people hear the teaching of the supreme ultimate truth, they are struck with alarm, doubt, and terror, as if falling into a deep pit.
Śāriputra, there are bhikṣus who delight in such matters; they gather together and destroy the unsurpassed bodhi of all Buddhas.

At that time, those with overweening pride and biased attachments will be numerous; furthermore, evil Māras will delude the minds of both householders and renunciants, causing them to cling to what is not the Dharma.
When those who preach the True Dharma have little assistance, they will then disperse and perish, unable to remain established. "Śāriputra!
At that time, there will be many young bhikṣus in the world who possess sharp faculties."
Why is this? Those who have left the household life may still possess residual afflictions; yet, upon being reborn among humans, they once again renounce the world.
These bhikṣus delight in posing difficult questions, seeking the foremost ultimate truth of the Buddha-dharma.

Śāriputra! At that time, those with overweening pride, deluded by Māra and seeking only to sustain their lives, were in fact ordinary worldlings who called themselves Arhats. They spoke to the young bhikṣus and others, saying:
"Virtue in body, speech, and mind—this is the foremost, ultimate truth of the Buddha-dharma."

To well-guard the pure precepts, to recite the sutras and dharmas, and to diligently cultivate extensive learning—these are called the causes and conditions for the "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti), namely, purifying the mind and placing faith in the Buddha.

Furthermore, there is the foremost ultimate truth: you should bind your mind to its object and single-mindedly contemplate nirvana as the cessation of the three kinds of suffering; thus, you will be able to develop weary detachment toward the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.

"You should, in a quiet place, contemplate how these phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are all impermanent; observe your own body as being variously impure. If you can contemplate in this way, you shall attain the fruit of srotāpanna."

Furthermore, if one can deeply contemplate these dharmas, such as the five aggregates, as impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and lacking solidity, one attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin; by contemplating them even more deeply, one attains Anāgāmin and Arhatship—this is the primary ultimate truth.
Then the young bhikṣu asked again:
"Within the Buddha-dharma, is the fruit of arhatship indeed the ultimate truth?
We also know this: that attaining arhatship is the ultimate truth."
"Now, regarding these five aggregates, do they arise for one who possesses mindfulness, or do they arise for one who lacks mindfulness?
He replied, "These five aggregates arise for one who possesses mindfulness; they do not arise for one who lacks mindfulness."
He asked again:
"Do you consider mindfulness to be different from the five aggregates?
He replied:
"Just as it is with the five aggregates, so it is with mindfulness.
He asked again:
"If it is just as it is with the five aggregates, so it is with mindfulness, then who is it that is mindful of the five aggregates?"
He replied:
"If there were no one who contemplates the five aggregates, there would be no nirvāṇa;
because there truly are those who contemplate the five aggregates, there are therefore those who cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path and enter nirvāṇa."
“Śāriputra! In future ages, there will be many bhikṣus who achieve this patience. Śāriputra!”
At that time, there were many members of the assembly among the devas who wished to hear the foremost ultimate truth of the Buddha-dharma.
Upon hearing what these people of overweening pride had said, their minds were filled with doubt and regret as if they had fallen into a deep pit, and they all spoke thus:
"Alas! How tragic!"
"The Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha is now about to perish swiftly.
Śāriputra! Among them, there will be bhikṣus who have accomplished roots of goodness; these bhikṣus will say:
"Foolish man, you are empty of old age, a person of overweening pride.

If there were any signs of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, or the eighteen elements, he would not accept these words; being neither pleased nor delighted, he would rise from his seat and depart.
Śāriputra! At that time, the hearts of all the devas were filled with great joy, and they proclaimed in the four directions:

"The Buddha Śākyamuni still has excellent disciples remaining; these people possess no small amount of roots of goodness, for they do not take pleasure in hearing such impure teachings as these, namely:"
"The views of self and the views of a person.

When the devas heard this, they were all greatly delighted; they extolled and praised this one of sharp faculties, rejoicing that through his inquiries and challenges, he would surely achieve the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Such people as these gather in one place to form a band; since the number of people is small, their power is also weak.
"Śāriputra! At that time, my true sons..."
If they do not even speak kindly toward their own paternal kin, how much less could they receive offerings or dwell in stūpas and monasteries?
Śāriputra, you should observe this:

at that time, the Tathāgata will already be slighted; likewise, after my parinirvāṇa, when my sons have attained the patient endurance of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-kṣānti*) and peaceful tranquility, they too will be treated with contempt.

For this reason, throughout incalculable kalpas, I have subdued all enemies and transformed all celestial kings and human kings so that their minds became pure; the purpose of doing so was to enable my sons to attain the position of father.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata now takes all the gods and humans of the world as witnesses that the Tathāgata has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in accordance with the Dharma and has turned the unsurpassed wheel of the Dharma—
a wheel which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, god, Māra, or Brahmā can turn.

“Śāriputra! Regarding this present matter, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, when my disciples wish to widely propagate this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of mine, these evil persons will be unable to provide testimony for it, nor will they be able to grant them fearlessness.”
“Śāriputra! It is like a jar of honey placed at a crossroads, with this proclamation:
‘If anyone can eat even as much as the tip of a single hair, they shall never grow old or die.’”
At that time, the devas and the people of the world each guarded this flask with swords and staves.
Those who were guarding it all spoke these words:
"If there should be anyone who eats even a single hair's tip from it, we shall kill them."
"Śāriputra! Among them, one person secretly thought to himself:
'If one eats even a hair’s tip of the honey in this jar, one will not grow old or die; why should I now begrudge death and not eat it?'"
‘If I obtain it and eat it, I shall no longer fear my guards, and I may also forever be free from old age, sickness, and death.
With his mind thus fixed in concentration, he disregarded his life and went straight to where the jar was. The guards, each wielding a sword or staff, vied with one another to kill him.
"Śāriputra!
If this person can prevent even a single drop from being consumed by sword or staff, they shall escape decline and affliction, and no longer undergo old age and death.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!"
There will be many wicked people, Māras, and the followers of Māra who wish to extinguish my Dharma.

After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, if there are those who can accord with the dharma of emptiness, penetrating it without doubt, they will have no attainment regarding any phenomena in their minds and will achieve supreme patience (adhimātra-kṣānti).

At that time, although they may be slighted and their path obstructed by evil persons, if such people can practice with diligence and vigor, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives, and penetrate the fact that all phenomena are without arising and without activity, they will attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
“Śāriputra! This jar of honey is the Buddha’s Dharma of the ultimate meaning (paramārtha).

Those gods and worldly people who guard this jar are actually evil persons who delight in performing the works of Māra; they lose their own great benefit and also obstruct others who practice the true mark (lakṣaṇa), causing them to lose their great benefit.”

"Śāriputra! Those with overweening pride are all partisans of Māra who assist in accomplishing the works of Māra; they all join together in deriding and reviling the dharma that is without arising or ceasing.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Those who speak of impurity—those with views of a self, a person, a sentient being, and views regarding the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements; those who claim to have attained what they have not attained, whose minds reckon they have attained the Way and reckon they have attained Nirvana—all such persons likewise revile and slander this True Dharma.
Why is this? Because such persons are greedily attached to emptiness; they belong to the host of Māras, are deluded by Māra, and perform the works of Māra under the guise of my True Dharma.

“Śāriputra! If those, whether lay or ordained, who hear this teaching of non-self, no person, no sentient being, and ultimate emptiness, become startled, doubtful, or fearful, you should know that such persons have been converted by Māra; they are counterfeit bhikṣus and are practitioners of evil conduct who steal the Dharma.”

Śāriputra! Such a person possesses the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, the view of permanence, and the view of annihilation; they are all subjects of Māra and not disciples of the Buddha.
Why is this? In my sūtras I have said: "All worlds are empty;

they are without self and without what belongs to a self; they are without a person, without a sentient being; they are impermanent and unstable; there is no phenomenon that is not subject to destruction."

"Such evil persons likewise all together read and recite this sutra and explain it to others, yet their minds are greedily attached to the view of self and the view of a person. Such deluded people are called those who create the causes of suffering; they are called those who waver between two extremes; they are called those who cause strife and schism within the Sangha; they are called those who defile the Dharma; they are called the turbidity among śramaṇas; they are called the ugly and the foul; they are called those who possess only empty words; they are called false śramaṇas; they are called the poor among śramaṇas; they are called those who carry a heavy burden; they are called those who deceive and mislead the Buddhas; and they are called those who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution."
“Śāriputra! Such a person is called a great and wicked rebel; he is called a bad friend (pāpamitra); he is called one who has broken the precepts;
he is called one of wrong views; he is called a non-Buddhist (tīrthika); he is called one lacking true practice; he is called an evil companion.”

...called the "Killing Ghost," called "Leprosy," called "Foul Stench," called "Burning Heat," called "Deceit and Crookedness," called "Falling into Darkness," called "Entering the Thicket of the Forest," called "Falling into the Stream of Birth and Death," called "Mutually Producing Evil," called "Hell," and named...
They are called animals; they are called hungry ghosts; they are called asuras; they are called those who do not enter the Path;
they are called those who deceive others; they are called those who praise themselves; they are called those who practice divination and physiognomy;
they are called those who shout out at great volume; they are called those who seek profit through profit; they are called defilers.
One who defiles the families of others is called one who is constantly engaged in frivolous play; one is called one with a distracted mind;
one is called one harmed by greed; one is called one harmed by hatred; one is called one harmed by delusion;
one is called one who delights in deceiving others with a pleasant countenance; one is called one who dwells in decline and affliction; and one is called one who lacks liberation.
They are called those bound by the fetters of distress;

they are called non-śramaṇas who merely have the appearance of śramaṇas, śramaṇa-cāṇḍālas, foul-smelling śramaṇas, dregs of śramaṇas; they are called those difficult to satisfy, those difficult to support, those who have ruined their dignified conduct, those who are shameless, those whose heads are severed, those whose bodies are ruined, those who wear the kāṣāya around their necks, those who enter into darkness themselves, those with much greed, those with much anger, those with much delusion, those entangled and covered by the five hindrances, those who are submerged, those who are vain and empty, and those who are foolish.
"Śāriputra, what is meant by 'emptiness'?
Because one has fallen away from the marks of a person praised as virtuous by all Buddhas, it is called emptiness."
Because one has fallen away from all the merits of a śramaṇa and the dharmas pertaining to the work of a śramaṇa, it is called "empty.
What is meant by "false"?
Because one stands outside the noble Dharma, it is called "false."
Because they distance themselves from the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they are called "vain.

Śāriputra, such evil persons cause Māra to rejoice; because they greedily cling to and stubbornly adhere to false and illusory dharmas, they are identical to ordinary worldlings and fully possess the characteristics of sinful people.
Those who do not resemble those who have attained the patience of dharma possess not even one part in a hundred thousand million of the dharma-work of a śramaṇa or the merit of a śramaṇa.
Śāriputra! For this reason, they are called "empty" and "vain."

They are merely deeply attached to worldly profit and pleasure; they are not true śramaṇas though they claim to be śramaṇas. They accept offerings that they do not deserve, and are called "constant thieves," "thieves who plant the banner of their craft," and "thieves who kill and harm others with impunity."

Every morsel of food consumed by this person is entirely impure; only those who have turned toward the Path and attained its fruits can digest such offerings. This person lacks these qualities; therefore, they are called one who consumes impure food.
Śāriputra! For this reason, they are called "empty" and "void.
What do you think?

If a person commits killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, greed, envy, anger, malice, and wrong views, is this person constantly killing and constantly taking life?
"No, World-Honored One!
A householder who kills does not constantly take life; the time he kills is brief, while the time he does not kill is great."
“Śāriputra, what do you think? When a person commits theft,
is the time of stealing more frequent, or the time of not stealing more frequent?”
“World-Honored One!
There are many times when one does not steal. “Śāriputra!”
"What do you think?
If a person engages in sexual misconduct, is the time spent in sexual misconduct more frequent, or is the time not spent in sexual misconduct more frequent?
"World-Honored One!"
"When is there more time spent in sexual misconduct?
When is there more time spent in lying, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, jealousy, and anger, as opposed to the time when one is free from anger?"
“World-Honored One!
The time when there is no anger is more frequent. “Śāriputra!”
"Among these ten unwholesome paths of action, which carries the heaviest offense?
"World-Honored One,
among the ten unwholesome actions, wrong view is the heaviest offense."
Why is this? World-Honored One!
Those with wrong views are constantly stained by defilements in their minds; thus, their minds are not pure.
“Śāriputra! I tell you now:

suppose there is a person who in a single day kills hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings; in a single day steals hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of gold, silver, and precious objects; who commits sexual misconduct without ceasing day or night;
and who speaks falsely, constantly deceiving others, with impure verbal karma such that not a single word is truthful.
The double-tongued person constantly breaks apart those in harmony and assists in their division;
the one of harsh speech has a mouth that is perpetually foul and rebellious, never uttering even a single word of gentleness;
the frivolous speaker lacks any foundation, and when asked about a certain matter, they confound it with countless other words.
Those who are covetous and envious give rise to unrighteous thoughts regarding the property of others;
those who harbor anger give rise to groundless resentment and malice that fills their hearts;
and those with wrong views delight in practicing unwholesome paths.
Śāriputra! What do you think?
If a person were to accomplish such unwholesome dharmas as these, would their transgression not be great?
“Very many, World-Honored One! “Śāriputra!

I tell you now: if a person were to commit these ten unwholesome offenses for a hundred years, the transgression of a precept-breaking bhikṣu who accepts offerings from others for a single day and night would be greater than that.

Why is this? This person who takes life is known by many and recognized by many; they are loathed and despised by people. Everyone knows that such a person is a killer and a plunderer of life, a sinner, defiled, and a polluter; they are unwholesome, devoid of virtue, and one whom people avoid.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A person who kills takes the lives of others; perhaps they develop a sense of revulsion and realize their own wrongdoing, knowing they will surely receive retribution for their sins. All people know such a person is evil, lacking precepts, and defiled; they do not expect even a hundredth part of a single hair’s worth of merit from them, much less regard them as a field of merit worthy of offerings.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

As for those who take life, everyone in their household—including their wives and children—knows of it and will not show them respect; they will not even allow them to sit, let alone provide them with offerings.

A person who has taken life may sustain themselves with wealth and support their wife and children, and at times may even make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; yet, as a result of this karma, they may encounter virtuous bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who preach the Dharma for them, instructing them to abstain from killing and abandon the karma of slaughter.

Within the Buddha-dharma, they shall encounter no obstacles in leaving the household life; having left the household life, they will draw near to spiritual friends and attain the fruits of the śramaṇa. Such persons will experience the retribution for their offenses lightly in this present life; it shall not obstruct the Noble Path, and they will be spared from the three miserable realms.

“Śāriputra! Within my Dharma there are certain bhikṣus who are not śramaṇas yet claim to be śramaṇas, and who do not practice the holy life (brahmacarya) yet claim to practice the holy life. They sever all roots of goodness, obstruct entry into nirvāṇa, and are deluded, losing the Way. They destroy the causes and conditions for the Way and ruin all wholesome dharmas; they perform the deeds of non-Buddhists and enter the evil realms.”

Amidst many evil bandits, those who draw breath in vain are like the dead; their physical forms are haggard and they have lost all proper decorum. Within my Dharma, they are called defilers, called thieves of the Dharma, called rebels, and called messengers of Māra.
They are like a walking latrine and like a dead dog; they are semblances of śramaṇas, wearing the robes of a śramaṇa but lacking the deeds of a śramaṇa.
"Śāriputra! They are like a jackal among a pride of lions."
It is like a eunuch among the assembly of a wheel-turning sage king;
it is like a monkey among the devas;
and it is also like a donkey among a herd of elephant kings.
They are like blind people among those with the divine eye;
they are like bats among the assembly of garuḍas. Śāriputra!

When a precept-breaking bhikṣu is among my assembly, and the great multitude of hundreds of thousands of millions of devas sees this bhikṣu sitting in the congregation, they all become deeply distressed and say:
"What use is there for a poṣadha ceremony with such an evil person?"
"These are followers of Māra who wish to hear of the unsurpassed Buddha-way and speak of it to laypeople.
Furthermore, there were various dragons, spirits, and deities who had faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, and they cried out in a loud voice at these evil bhikṣus:
"For what reason do you conceal your bodies here?"
"He is like a vicious horse among well-trained horses.

Thus, this deluded man claims that no one perceives his evil; he hides himself here, deceiving gods and humans. He is a thief among all these gods and humans, and when the multitude sees him, they all laugh even more loudly.

“Śāriputra! Such evil monks are known by these devas as wicked thieves; yet they receive offerings from laypeople no differently than [holy ones], being welcomed and seen off, prostrated to, and honored with palms joined.”

This wretched person is as foolish as a corpse; the clothes he wears are all stolen, the food he eats from his bowl is all taken by theft, and there is no one who gives him anything—not even a drop of water is obtained except through theft.
Śāriputra! To whatever region a precept-breaking bhikṣu goes—whether to the east, south, west, or north—he travels as one who treads upon stolen ground.

Why is this? All the modes of conduct and dharmas of such a person are produced through theft, deception, and pilfering. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; coming or going; looking or gazing; bending or stretching; bowing or raising the head; putting on robes or holding the alms bowl—now, to speak briefly of the actions of body, speech, and mind, whatever they perform is all the work of thieves. If anyone were to shave the hair of such a person, it would be to shave the hair of a thief.
To state the essentials: whatever a precept-breaking bhikṣu undertakes is all the work of a thief.
Śāriputra, even for a corrupt and evil bhikṣu, such acts as passing stool or urine and washing his hands are all the ways of a thief. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Within Jambudvīpa, all that belongs to kings, ministers, and the people, as well as that which is possessed by non-human beings, these wicked bhikṣus act as thieves therein.
“Śāriputra! If a king or his ministers do not expect merit from evil bandits, nor say they are equal to them, nor say they are superior to them;
yet, toward a precept-breaking bhikṣu who wears the noble dharma-robes, they expect to gain merit—therefore, they permit such a person to dwell within their realm.
If one knows their evil, even spitting upon the ground is not permitted.

Therefore, Śāriputra, whatever a corrupt and wicked bhikṣu does with his body is the work of a thief; he is called a constant thief, a great thief, a thief who plants the banner of defiance, and one who strikes and harms all people in the world.
Why is this? Because there is no evil they will not commit.
Therefore, Śāriputra!
Such evil bhikṣus are great thieves among all the worlds of devas and humans. Śāriputra,
if a person is a great thief among all the worlds of devas and humans, would such a person be able to digest even a single draught of water?
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"
"What do you think?
Is this person not a person of great evil? "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!
A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts incurs a great and grave offense within the entire world of devas and humans. For this reason, I have spoken this verse:”
"‘It would be better to eat burning stones and swallow molten copper than,
lacking precepts, to consume the faithful offerings of others. Śāriputra!"

This precept-breaking bhikṣu lacks physical beauty and virtue, and is devoid of further aspiration. His body and mind are scorched by poisonous heat, and he delights in seeing evil dreams; he finds no joy in solitary dwelling. Whether he dwells alone at times or walks alone, his body trembles with fear.
Upon seeing those of pure precepts, they hide themselves away and turn aside; their hearts are timid and filled with self-reproach, and they take no pleasure in seeing them.
When receiving offerings, they are startled, suspicious, and terrified; their minds are constantly racing with manifold thoughts, deeply craving wealth and profit, and delighting in fine food.
"Thus it is, bhikṣu!
After the end of his life, he will certainly enter hell.
Śāriputra!"
These are called the seven arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu, who will inevitably enter hell.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu delights in noisy crowds, is distracted and talkative by nature, and is prone to jealousy. He makes friends with those who break the precepts, constantly delights in discussing the evil deeds of those who break the precepts, and takes such things as his pleasure without knowing shame. He opposes the profound sūtras, harboring doubts and refusing to believe."

At times, when hearing the exposition of such sūtras as these, they harbor doubts, resist, and contend, taking no pleasure in listening or receiving them; they look here and there with their minds undivided, cover their mouths with their hands, gaze up at the empty sky, rise from their seats, slander the Buddha’s Dharma teachings, and with hearts full of resentment, revile the teacher of the Dharma.
Due to such causes and conditions of transgression and evil, after the end of their lives, they will sink deep into hell.
Śāriputra! These are called the eight arrows of grief and affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu; they will certainly fall into hell.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu delights only in honoring his upādhyāya and ācārya, seeking fame and profit by praising their virtues; he claims to uphold the precepts as a means of livelihood, and when performing administrative duties, he acts with expedient compliance and skillfulness, yet remains devoid of shame, just like a black crow."

For the sake of the Saṃgha, he sought out clothing and food excessively; his mouth and body indulged in such abundance that he became stout and robust. Lacking a sense of shame and modesty, his speech was incoherent and lacked order.
His hands and feet were coarse and dry, and his complexion was haggard and withered. He delighted in gazing at women and did not associate with men.
Such evil persons are despised by the multitude and are not praised by devas, nāgas, or spirits; even the Buddhas do not extol them.
Their mental nature is impetuous and they constantly delight in anger; when the Saṃgha adjudicates matters, they act with partisan force.

Śāriputra! Such precept-breaking bhikṣus mostly seek to gain power and influence within the Saṃgha; they answer before being questioned and constantly seek out the faults of others, regarding those who maintain pure precepts as being deceitful.
Those who diligently seek the Way do not share their methods; those who delight in discord and dispute encourage such strife. Śāriputra!
These are called the nine arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu, by which he will surely fall into hell.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu delights in the affairs of others and takes charge of their management;

he finds joy in those who engage in quarrels and disputes. He adorns his body with robes and imitates the deportment of others. He seeks fine bedding, requisites, and gain for the sake of securing his own comfort and seeking the praise of others. He guards the offerings of donors and begrudges his dwelling place. Fearing that virtuous bhikṣus might come to see his faults, he hates those who uphold the precepts and attaches himself to those who break them."
They constantly praise giving, but do not praise ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, or wisdom; nor do they praise tranquility, seclusion, or dwelling in solitude.

They constantly delight in criticizing those who uphold the precepts and fail to praise those who practice the dhūta austerities; they may point out their faults, speak with harsh words, or falsely speak based on mere conjecture.

Relying on their kinship and lineage, they frequently inquire after their relatives; for minor reasons, they preach the Dharma out of greed; always harboring suspicion with a crooked mind, they are detested by the multitude and increasingly despised over time.

They constantly delight in disparaging those who uphold the precepts; they do not wish to associate with those who speak words that are harsh yet true, nor do they take pleasure in hearing such sūtras as these.
They dislike seeing those who enjoy upholding, reading, and reciting such sūtras, or even those whose hearts rejoice when these sūtras are preached.

Furthermore, they take no pleasure in hearing praise of the dharma of upholding the precepts; when these kinds of sūtras are preached, they do not come to listen or receive them, and even if they do come to listen and receive them, they depart shortly thereafter.

They frequently associate with laypeople as their companions and always delight in discussing monks who uphold the precepts. Having attained a sense of self-indulgence, they act with negligence and commit violent evils.
“Śāriputra! These are called the ten arrows of affliction for a precept-breaking bhikṣu; he will certainly fall into the evil realms. Śāriputra!”
"After my parinirvāṇa, people such as these will fill Jambudvīpa, making their living solely by seeking profit.
**Chapter Six: On Pure Dharmas (Middle Section)** *The Buddha-Store Sūtra*, Chapter Six: On Pure Dharmas The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"In the past, Kāśyapa Buddha predicted concerning me, saying:"
"Because Śākyamuni Buddha accepts many offerings, his Dharma shall quickly perish.
"Śāriputra! It is true that because my Dharma receives many offerings, it shall later quickly perish."
Śāriputra! It is like a poor person who, upon finding a great treasure trove, experiences immense joy.
In the same way, Śāriputra!

In future ages, there will be many bhikṣus who associate closely with laypeople and accept their offerings; gradually becoming intimate and acting as their attendants, they will feel joy in their hearts and take it for pleasure, just like a poor man who finds a great treasure trove.
Such deluded people value worldly gain and the pleasures of servitude.
When they see a bhikṣu receiving offerings from many people, they immediately think he has attained arhatship; yet when they see one with few acquaintances, they call him a wicked man.
"Thus it is, Bhikṣu!
For the sake of gain and offerings, you have abandoned the supreme path of the Buddha; whatever you now desire, you shall accomplish it. Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgata now preaches such sūtras as these for the sake of these deluded people.

Why is this? When a bhikṣu who has broken the precepts hears this sūtra being preached, he will give rise to a mind of repentance and shall return to upholding the precepts, no longer acting as a great thief while receiving the offerings of others.
Śāriputra! If there are bhikṣus who, upon hearing this sutra, have minds that are not pure, nor joyful, nor delighted, these are called wicked and evil bhikṣus.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
for a bhikṣu of pure precepts, there is no dharma that he does not delight in.

Whether they speak of generosity, or speak of ethical discipline, or speak of patience, or speak of diligence, or speak of meditative concentration, or speak of wisdom; or whether they speak of such sūtras and teachings on revulsion and fear, their minds are always filled with joy and delight.
“Śāriputra! There are three kinds of people whose minds become distressed and troubled upon hearing this sutra preached.
What are these three?
First, monks who have broken the precepts; second, those with overweening pride; third, those who preach the Dharma impurely.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of people whose minds become distressed and troubled upon hearing such a sutra as this.
What are the three?
First, the view of a person; second, the view of a life-force; and third, the view of a self. “Śāriputra!

I now declare this clearly to you: like a good spiritual friend who, with a heart of compassion, seeks benefit, happiness, and peace for others, you should all listen to my words with a single mind, constantly seeking wholesome benefit and never being negligent.
“Śāriputra, there are five faults for one who teaches the Dharma impurely.
What are these five?
First, they claim to know all the Buddha’s teachings;
second, when expounding the Buddha’s sutras, they point out contradictions and faults within those scriptures;
third, they harbor doubts and lack faith regarding the various dharmas.
Fourth, they rely on what they themselves know rather than the teachings of other scriptures;
fifth, they preach the Dharma to others for the sake of gain and offerings. Śāriputra!
Regarding those who speak in such a manner, I say that these persons shall fall into hell and shall not attain nirvāṇa.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma is among a great assembly, those who have faith and delight in the Dharma prepare a high seat for him; yet this person abandons the Buddha’s true Dharma to preach the ornate rhetoric of external paths—[thinking], 'I have long striven with hardship to seek this jewel of the Dharma, yet this evil person sets it aside and does not preach it. Instead, using words and meanings from the sūtras that are contradictory, they engage in mutual refutation and affirmation, failing to accord with the true Dharma. Within the noble Dharma, they harbor haughty pride and preach according to their own whims in order to seek gain and offerings."

Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma while intermingling it with the doctrines of external paths, a virtuous bhikṣu who diligently seeks the Way should rise from his seat and depart. Why is this?
Śāriputra! When a layperson with faith has prepared a high seat, one should not expound the words and meanings of non-Buddhist paths;
if one does not depart, they are not a virtuous bhikṣu, nor can they be called one who follows the Buddha’s teachings.
Śāriputra! To preach the Dharma is exceedingly difficult; one who speaks in such a manner, I declare, is a follower of the heterodox Nirgrantha, not a disciple of the Buddha.
After this Dharma-preacher has passed away, he shall be reborn in the path of the Nirgranthas.
What is the path of the Nirgranthas?
Wrong view is the path of the Nirgranthas.
What constitutes wrong view?
It refers to [the realms of] hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts. Why is this so?
"Śāriputra!
If one occupies a high seat without having personally realized the Dharma, and teaches others while remaining ignorant oneself, such a person will surely fall into hell. Śāriputra!"
The Tathāgata fully knows such causes and conditions: that my disciples, by means of various gateways, various causes and conditions, and various views, will cause the extinction of my True Dharma.

Śāriputra! If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this sūtra on the ultimate truth of emptiness and the dharma of non-existence, feel joy in their hearts, you should know that such persons are truly my disciples.

“Śāriputra! In a past age, there were five hundred blind men traveling along a road who reached a great city and were utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst. They sent one blind man outside to guard their belongings while the others entered the city to beg for food and drink.”
Before long, a certain deceiver went to where the guardian was and said, "Hey, man!
Why are you staying here alone?
He replied:
"I have many companions entering the city to beg for alms.
He spoke these words to deceive the man: "Do you know?"
In that place, food, clothing, necklaces, flowers, perfumes, and various articles are available for great distribution at will; if you require them, I shall take you there.
He replied, "So be it!
Then the deceiver led the blind man away a short distance from his original spot and seized all of his belongings.
Having received their alms, the blind beggars returned; deceiving the people, they spoke again to the other blind men, saying:
"Did you all receive the offerings from the great assembly?
They replied:
"No," he replied, deceiving them by saying:
"Place whatever you have obtained here; I shall lead you to the Great Assembly for Almsgiving."
The blind men all together left their belongings in one place and followed the deceiver away.
When they reached a great deep pit, the deceiver led all five hundred blind men there and said to them:
"This ground is level and excellent; there is a great assembly for almsgiving. Each of you should turn your faces toward the east and receive the offerings from others."
"Immediately they all fell into the pit and died. Śāriputra!

In the future, there will be bhikṣus who delight in reading external scriptures; when they preach the Dharma, they will embellish their prose and rhetoric to entertain the assembly, while at that time, evil Māras will assist in deluding the people and obstructing the wholesome Dharma."

If there are those who are greedily attached to sounds, speech, and elegant literary embellishments, or if there are others who delight in reading the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths, Māra will delude them all, causing their minds to feel at ease.
If there are bhikṣus who cultivate the Buddha-dharma, they cause them to give rise to doubt and confusion, leading all people to no longer provide them with offerings.

Or, if there are bhikṣus who have already read the Buddhist sūtras two or three times, they cause them to seek out the scriptures and teachings of external paths, praising those things they previously examined themselves as being "excellent."

These people, deluded and obscured by Māra, have their eye of wisdom covered; they greedily crave gain and profit and study various external scriptures, just like a group of blind men deceived by a fraud, all of whom are caused to fall into a deep pit and die.

Śāriputra! Those born blind are like bhikṣus who abandon the unsurpassed path of the Buddha to seek the scriptures of external paths; they deceive people as evil Māras, and the deep pit is the false path.
Śāriputra! It is like a group of blind men who, having abandoned the goods they had obtained, desire to go to a great feast but fall into a deep pit;

my disciples are just like this. Having abandoned coarse food and clothing, they pursue the "great feast" by seeking fine offerings; for the sake of worldly gain, they lose their great wisdom and fall into the deep pit of the Avīci Hell.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, those who preach the Dharma with impurity do not understand the Tathāgata’s intentional meaning (*abhiprāya*) as it adapts to circumstances; they explain it to others based on their own poor understanding. Such persons incur five faults in this present life, which others do not recognize."
This is known only to bhikṣus who have attained the divine eye and to the various devas.
What are these five?
First, when preaching the Dharma, one harbors fear in the heart, fearing that others will challenge or refute me.
2. Internally harboring sorrow and fear while externally speaking to others;
3. Being an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) lacking true wisdom;
4. What is spoken being impure, consisting merely of verbal expressions.
Fifth, their speech lacks sequence and consists of haphazard excerpts; therefore, when among the assembly, they harbor fear in their hearts.

Such ordinary persons lack wisdom and possess no certainty of mind; driven merely by the minor causes and conditions of pride, they seek fame and reputation. With doubt and regret in their hearts, they preach to others, whereby these people for a long night receive for themselves the poisonous arrows of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Why is this? Śāriputra, such a person cannot definitively know all dharmas, yet they preach them to others; their mind finds no joy in them, and even if they find joy, it is quickly lost.
“Śāriputra! I know that there is this fault in preaching the Dharma with impurity, whereby one does not attain the Right Path; all the bhikṣus do not know this, nor do the devas; only I know it.”
Furthermore, there are bhikṣus who preach the Dharma with impurity; they do not understand that which the Tathāgata has taught according to what is appropriate, yet they preach it to others.

While in the various sūtras there is no self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span, these individuals, relying on their own polemical rhetoric, claim that there is a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
This constitutes slandering the Buddha, slandering the Dharma, and slandering the Sangha—the sin of slandering the Triple Gem.
It is something that neither gods nor worldly people can know; only the Buddha knows it.
Śāriputra! Such a person is also called one who preaches the Dharma impurely.
I know their transgression, yet none of those with supernormal powers nor the hosts of devas can know it; only a Buddha knows it.
“Śāriputra! I shall now provide you with an analogy to explain this.
If a person, not knowing the meaning and characteristics of the Buddha-way, preaches the Dharma impurely to others, how many unwholesome deeds does such a person accomplish?”
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Are the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa many or not?
“Very much so,
World-Honored One! “Śāriputra!
“If there were an evil person who took the lives of all of them, would that person’s transgression not be very great?
“It would be very great,
World-Honored One!”
"Such a deluded person does not understand the Buddha-way, yet they preach the Dharma impurely to others;
their transgression is greater than this. Why is that?
Such a person preaches the Dharma with impurity, thereby destroying the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, and they also slander the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
If there were any Buddhas of the past who taught that all phenomena are ultimately empty, being without self, without person, without sentient beings, without a life-principle, and without a soul.
Śāriputra! The Buddhas of the future will also teach that all dharmas are ultimately empty, being without self, without person, without sentient beings, without life-force, and without a soul.
Śāriputra!

Now, in the present, the Buddhas in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions also teach that all dharmas are ultimately empty, being without self, without person, without sentient beings, without a life-principle, and without a soul.

Śāriputra! This is called the unsurpassed Dharma of all Buddhas; that is to say, all dharmas have no intrinsic nature and are unobtainable emptiness; their original nature is quiescent, without arising or ceasing, and devoid of essence, characteristics, or self-characteristics—all are empty.
The Tathāgata speaks only for the purpose of severing all recollections, thoughts, and discriminations; yet, the Bodhi of all Buddhas is without discrimination.
"Śāriputra, what is meant by discrimination?

What are called "discriminations" are the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of a soul, the view of annihilation, and the view of permanence; ordinary worldlings are established in all these discriminations.

If a person is free from such conceptual discrimination, they are able to fully understand that all phenomena are empty, devoid of a self, devoid of a person, devoid of a sentient being, devoid of a life-sustainer, and devoid of a vital principle.
When one contemplates in this way, the mind attains joy; hearing the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), one is neither startled nor afraid.

Such a person then knows that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are false and devoid of reality, and knows that the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) and eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are false and devoid of reality.
This person also does not discriminate regarding nirvāṇa, does not think of nirvāṇa, and does not say, "I am able to contemplate nirvāṇa.
Because they attain quiescence through the Dharma, they do not discriminate; as for that state of quiescence reached by this Dharma, they neither discriminate it nor apprehend it.
Śāriputra! This is called the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti).
Within this ultimate meaning of the patience of conformity, that person likewise does not apprehend any self-characteristic.
Śāriputra! What is the characteristic of the patient acceptance that accords with reality?
It is said that the signless is the characteristic of the patient acceptance that accords with reality.
“Śāriputra, what do you think?

If a person does not even perceive the marks of this ‘patience in accordance with reality,’ it is impossible for that person to perceive a self-mark, a person-mark, a sentient-being-mark, a life-span-mark, or a living-being-mark.”
If a person accomplishes such wisdom, they should receive offerings; this one is called a son of the Buddha, and is called one who has entered the non-abiding samādhi. "Śāriputra!

This is called the gateway to the ultimate meaning of the Buddha-dharma, which is characterized by the absence of recollective conceptualization and discrimination, and the absence of "this" and "that.
Yet these deluded people, in the midst of a great assembly, preach false views, using their own recollective conceptualization and discrimination to instruct others:
"This is the Buddha-dharma; this is the Noble Path."
Such a deluded person thus slanders the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Such a deluded person is called an evil friend (pāpamitra), not a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).

Śāriputra! Although an enemy may take one’s life, it results only in the loss of a single body; yet such a deluded person who teaches the Dharma impurely causes great ruin and affliction for all sentient beings for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.

This person is deluded and ignorant, obscuring the Buddha’s bodhi; their original mind of craving and attachment flares up once more, continuing without interruption. Because of this craving and attachment, they wander through the five realms of existence, lacking any virtuous path, and the cycle of birth and death remains unceasing.
Therefore, Śāriputra, those who preach the Dharma impurely incur exceedingly great demerit; they act as evil friends to sentient beings and slander the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.

“Śāriputra! Setting aside the sentient beings of this Jambudvīpa, if someone were to take the lives of all beings in a trichiliocosm, the sin of preaching the Dharma with impurity would be greater than that.”

Why is this? Because these people destroy the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas and assist the works of Māra; they also cause sentient beings to undergo various decays and afflictions for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes. They are only able to create bonds and cannot bring about liberation. One should know that such people act as evil friends (*pāpa-mitra*) to all sentient beings and are speakers of falsehoods; they slander and revile the Buddhas in the midst of the great assembly. Due to these causes and conditions, they fall into the great hells, and by teaching many sentient beings through the matters of false views, they are therefore called those with evil and perverse views.

Śāriputra! Those who hold views of a self, views of a person, or views of a sentient being mostly fall into false views; those who hold the view of annihilation mostly attain the Way quickly. Why is this?
Because it is easy to abandon [such faults].
Therefore, you should know that this person would rather cut out their own tongue with a sharp blade than preach the Dharma impurely in the midst of the assembly.
Chapter Seven: The Ancient Past The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Mahāvyūha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
That Buddha’s lifespan will be sixty-eight million billion years, and he will have a community of sixty-eight million billion great disciples.

After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his relics will be distributed just as they are after my own parinirvāṇa, without any difference; the True Dharma will also remain in the world for five hundred years, just as it does after my own parinirvāṇa, without any difference.

After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among his great assembly of disciples, on a single day there were a hundred bhikṣus who entered nirvāṇa; there were two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred who entered nirvāṇa; and on some days, there might be ten trillion bhikṣus who entered nirvāṇa within a single day.
In this manner, through successive transmission, the entire assembly of that Buddha’s great disciples—possessing vast knowledge and great supernormal powers—all entered nirvana within three months.
"Śāriputra!..."
The True Dharma of the Buddha Mahāvyūha was widely disseminated, and he was honored by many devas and humans.

Śāriputra, after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Mahāvyūha and his great disciples, there gradually arose many people who knew that the dharma of the śramaṇas is peaceful and blissful, and they left home to study the Way; yet they were unable to understand the peerless meaning of emptiness in the profound sūtras expounded by the Buddha, and for the most part, they were deluded by evil Māras.

At that time, the teacher of the Dharma was not resolute in mind and did not speak with purity; he spoke of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life span, and did not teach that all dharmas are empty and quiescent.
One hundred years after that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his assembly of disciples was divided into five schools:
the first was named Pǔshì (Universal Service);
the second was named Kù'àn (Bitter Shore).
The third was Sādhaka;
the fourth was Upacāru;
the fifth was Upananda.
“Śāriputra! These five bhikṣus—Bhikṣu Viśvāmitra, Bhikṣu Duḥkhakūla, Bhikṣu Sādhaka, Bhikṣu Nandika, and Bhikṣu Upananda—are teachers of the great assembly.”

As for that Universal Servant (Viśvāmitra), he understood the true meaning of emptiness and the dharma of non-apprehension as taught by the Buddha; the other four bhikṣus all followed false paths, frequently asserting the existence of a self and frequently asserting the existence of a person.
Śāriputra! The bhikṣu Samantakāraka was held in contempt by the fourfold assembly; he possessed no power and was loathed by many.

These four types of evil bhikṣus frequently instructed the masses in the path of false views; because they lacked mutual respect within the Buddha-dharma and acted in opposition to one another, they caused the extinction of the Buddha-dharma.
"Śāriputra!

If there is anyone who understands the Dharma of emptiness taught by the bhikṣu Pùshì, and accepts it with faith without opposition, I know that this person has, in previous lives, made offerings to five thousand Buddhas, and that sixty-eight billion nayutas of people have already entered nirvāṇa."

Why is this? Śāriputra, this person has planted roots of goodness under various Buddhas in past lives; having cultivated the dharma of emptiness characterized by non-apprehension, they are destined to enter nirvāṇa.

“Śāriputra! These bhikṣus—Dukkhakūla, Sabbakāmin, Ajita, and Upananda—all reckon that there is something to be attained; they assert the existence of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span, and their followers are numerous and flourishing.”

These four types of evil persons frequently cause householders and renunciants to dwell in false views; they cause them to abandon the ultimate truth of non-existence and ultimate emptiness, and instead greedily delight in the doctrines of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas.
Śāriputra! All the lay and ordained disciples of these four evil persons will constantly follow them until the Dharma comes to an end. Śāriputra!

Among these people, there are those who recognize an unrighteous matter, yet accept it as the Dharma and practice it with diligent mind; even so, they do not attain the patience that accords with truth (anulomikī kṣānti), much less the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna-phala).
Such people are not even capable of performing the act of consuming offerings, let alone being able to give rise to compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*). "Śāriputra!

At that time, many disciples, whether lay or ordained, will fall into evil realms and fail to reach the good realms. These wicked people will destroy the Buddha’s True Dharma and bring great ruin and affliction upon many others."
Furthermore, after these evil people die, they fall into the Avīci Hell, where they lie on their backs for nine hundred million *koṭis* of years;
they lie face down for nine hundred million *koṭis* of years;
and they lie on their left side for nine hundred million *koṭis* of years.
They lie on their right sides for nine hundred trillion years, burning, scorching, and rotting upon hot iron.

When they die there, they are reborn in the Hell of Roasting, the Great Hell of Roasting, the Reviving Hell, and the Black Rope Hell, where they undergo various sufferings for the same number of years as mentioned above. Upon dying in the Black Rope Hell, they are reborn once again within the Avīci Great Hell.
Śāriputra!

For these reasons, those who—whether laypeople or renunciants—have associated with this person, as well as his spiritual friends and all the donors, numbering six million four hundred thousand billion people in total, were born and died together with these four teachers, and are now undergoing various forms of burning and boiling in the great hells.
In this way, Śāriputra,
all those who belong to the families of this person’s virtuous friends and donors, as well as his disciples, teachers, and followers— all who are numbered among them— will be born in hell.

“Śāriputra! You and the others cannot know their number; only the Tathāgata can know it. There are six hundred and forty trillion people who, together with these evil persons, fall into the great hell, being born and dying there simultaneously. They undergo suffering in this manner for an entire kalpa, remaining in hell because the great kalpa is about to be consumed by fire.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the transgression of destroying the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of the Tathāgatas is extremely grave and not slight.

When the great kalpa is consumed by fire, these four evil persons and six hundred and forty trillion people will pass away from this Great Avīci Hell and be reborn in other regions within the great hells.
Why is this? Śāriputra, those who are fully possessed of grave offenses receive no small retribution;

they undergo great suffering for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of years in other worlds. When that world comes to an end, these four offenders, along with six hundred and forty trillion people and others whose offenses remain unexpiated, pass away there and are reborn here in this very Great Hell.

“Śāriputra! These four criminals and six hundred and forty trillion sentient beings, though they shall eventually escape the sufferings of hell and be born among humans, will be blind from birth for five hundred lifetimes. Only thereafter will they encounter the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān named Sarvāloka.”
Śāriputra! All the śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha Sarvābhāsvara numbered one hundred million nayutas.
At that time, the height of the people was three hundred and ninety-six cubits; the Buddha’s body was twice that size, and his constant radiance shone perfectly throughout ten trillion yojanas.

Śāriputra! Although this person has left the household life within all the luminous Buddha-dharmas and has practiced with diligent vigor for a hundred thousand *koṭis* of years as if his head were on fire, he does not even attain the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*), much less the fruits of the Path.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is the natural law that such karmic conditions for the offense of creating obstacles to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* must arise.
After their lives ended, they were reborn once again in the Great Avīci Hell due to the causes and conditions of the grave unwholesome karma they had previously committed. "Śāriputra!

These people continued to transmigrate in this manner until, during that interval, I encountered ninety-nine billion Buddhas, yet at the abodes of those Buddhas, I did not attain the patience of compliance (anulomikī-kṣānti)."

Why is this? Because such persons do not believe the profound sutras spoken by the Buddha; they destroy, oppose, and slander the noble ones and bhikṣus who uphold the precepts. By exposing their faults and evils, they create the causes and conditions for the karma of destroying the Dharma; it is only natural that the Dharma should be thus.
“Śāriputra! Behold this:
by slandering the noble ones and disbelieving the words of the noble ones, one undergoes immeasurable and boundless suffering and affliction, failing to attain liberation.”

Śāriputra! There are sentient beings who give rise to the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma, acting in opposition and lacking faith; their number is immeasurable, and throughout ninety-nine billion buddha-fields over asaṃkhyeya kalpas, not a single one among them has entered nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra! Who are those capable of destroying the teachings of all Buddhas by disbelieving and opposing them?
They are merely foolish worldlings, as well as evil bhikṣus of overweening pride, and those bhikṣus who preach the Dharma with impurity.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
these three kinds of people are not called practitioners, nor are they called attainers.
Because these people do not believe in the Tathāgata’s Dharma, they slander, oppose,
and resist it. "Śāriputra,
if you ask who this Bhikṣu Kūla was that preached the Dharma impurely?"
That foolish person is Devadatta.
As for whom you think is the bhikṣu Sarvāstivādin who preaches the Dharma impurely, that is the bhikṣu Kokālika.
Śāriputra! If you ask who that bhikṣu was who departed and preached the Dharma impurely,
it was none other than the bhikṣu Kāla.
"Śāriputra, as for whom you ask to be the bhikṣu Baddhālaka who preaches the Dharma impurely, he is none other than the naked ascetic Pārimanda."

You who think that at that time it was Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra who spoke of the Buddhas' bodhi with purity and according to reality, thereby benefiting immeasurable sentient beings, are mistaken. It was indeed he.
Regarding this purity that has been taught, those who have followed and studied it have encountered five thousand buddhas; sixty-eight billion nayutas of people have all already attained parinirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra! If one speaks the truth, who is the supreme Dharma teacher, the one who definitively resolves the meaning of the Dharma and teaches with purity?
You should say it is Pūrṇa.”
Śāriputra! Pūrṇa’s mind is settled and resolute; what he speaks is free from difficulty, and there is nothing in it that gives rise to doubt or debate. Śāriputra!
"If one speaks the truth, who is the Dharma-master of all causes and conditions?
One should say it is Pūrṇa, Śāriputra!"
Throughout his successive lifetimes, Pūrṇa constantly performed the work of a Buddha for the sake of sentient beings.

Within the teachings of ninety billion Buddhas, he constantly served as a Dharma teacher, expounding the Dharma with purity; in the presence of each of those Buddhas, he lived out his entire life-span, always practicing the pure conduct of brahmacarya and preaching the Dharma with purity.

Śāriputra! Pūrṇa also served as a Dharma teacher within the teachings of the six Buddhas; he also served as a great Dharma teacher within my own teaching, and having become an arhat, his mind attained liberation.
"If one were to speak truthfully, who has made offerings to the Buddhas in every lifetime and planted roots of goodness?
One should say it was Pūrṇa. Śāriputra!"
Within the teachings of ninety billion Buddhas, Pūrṇa diligently sought learning and mastered definitive discourse; he possessed profound wisdom.
For this reason, the Tathāgata declared him the foremost among all Dharma-preachers.
Śāriputra! If I were to speak of Pūrṇa’s merits for one day and one night, they would not be exhausted; even if I continued beyond one day and one night, they would still not be exhausted.

Why is this? Because Pūrṇa’s Dharma-giving is free from worldly motives and he does not crave gain or offerings; furthermore, the Dharma Master Pūrṇa has attained the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
"Except for the Tathāgata, there is none among all the worlds whose words and principles can surpass his.
Śāriputra, I now tell you:

if a person wishes to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and preach the Dharma for others, they shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit, and will also be able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings."
Śāriputra! If there are those who destroy, oppose, and do not believe in this Dharma, they will give rise to immeasurable causes and conditions for heavy offenses. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Evil brings its own retribution, and goodness brings its own retribution.
For this reason, I now entrust this sutra to you; you should expound and analyze it extensively for the fourfold assembly.
Śāriputra! If one hears this sutra and believes it with a joyful heart, one immediately attains immeasurable and boundless merit.
If one hears it but does not believe it and feels no joy, one immediately incurs immeasurable and boundless heavy transgressions.
Śāriputra! You should know that such a person is called a precept-breaking bhikṣu, one of overweening pride, or an impure teacher of the Dharma. Śāriputra!
If a person violates such teachings, they shall be born blind and without eyes in every lifetime.
Śāriputra, I now tell you clearly: what I have spoken now is not like a potter who cherishes his unfired clay vessels.
I now clearly and extensively expound for the fourfold assembly the Dharma of the ultimate emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
That which is firm remains; that which is not firm is destroyed. Why is this so?

Śāriputra! When the Buddha attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he does not preach the Dharma for those who hold wrong views or are evil people; he does not preach the Dharma for those who hold the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span.
Why is this? Because all such attachments are termed wrong views, Śāriputra!
In this way, those who hold views of a self and views of a person cannot attain even the patience of conformity (anulomikī-kṣānti), much less attain the fruits of the path. Śāriputra!

If those with views of a self, views of a person, views of a sentient being, views of a life-span, views of annihilationism, or views of eternalism were able to attain the patience of conformity or attain the fruits of the path, such a thing is impossible.

Therefore, Śāriputra, if a person possesses such views as these, I do not permit them to receive any offerings within my Dharma; they are not practitioners, nor are they attainers, but merely seek their own livelihood within my Dharma.
“Śāriputra! I say that when those of external paths wish to enter the Buddha-dharma, they should undergo a four-month probation. Why is this?

Śāriputra, many among the non-Buddhist practitioners hold views of a self, views of a person, views of a sentient being, views of a life-span, views of annihilationism, and views of eternalism. Śāriputra!
My disciples have no view of a self, no view of a person, no view of a sentient being, no view of a life-span, no view of annihilation, and no view of permanence. My disciples!
I speak only of the patience of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-apprehension, and I speak of consciousness having no place of abiding.

Śāriputra, if there are those who achieve such patience, I permit them to leave the household life and receive the precepts; they shall be permitted to receive offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine.
If there is a person who does not possess this patience, one should first test them by first instructing them to abide in the selflessness of all phenomena. Śāriputra!

If such a person feels no joy in this mind of patience, but instead becomes startled, suspicious, and critical upon hearing the teaching of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), yet feels joy in their heart upon hearing the teaching of the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), you should know that this person is either a servant of Māra or formerly belonged to the non-Buddhist paths.
“Śāriputra, a wise person should not give rise to sorrow regarding this; rather, they should give rise to a heart of compassion toward this individual. Why is that?

Śāriputra! If there are people who have accomplished such evils, the retribution they receive for those evils cannot be fully described. One should give rise to a mind of benefit toward these people and teach them that all phenomena are without self, that all phenomena are empty and quiescent, and that all phenomena are without action and without a recipient.

If such a person loves the Buddha-dharma and their heart rejoices upon hearing these matters, then the other bhikṣus who practice emptiness but have not yet attained realization should all instruct, benefit, gladden, and comfort them by explaining that all phenomena are non-existent and empty.

If they become startled or afraid upon hearing this, those bhikṣus should speak to their upādhyāya and ācārya within the assembly, as it is taught in the sūtras regarding those who practice the path of emptiness.

Furthermore, one who can discern the specific characteristics of all phenomena is my teacher; I do not take as a teacher one who holds views of self, views of a person, inverted false views, or those who are greedily attached to the observance of precepts.

“The Tathāgata permits those who possess right view to perform the poṣadha together, but he does not permit those who have broken the precepts, those with wrong views, or those who have violated the rules of decorum to perform the poṣadha together.”

When the elder disciples hear the teaching on emptiness, quiescence, and non-existence, their minds lack faith and joy, and they set their aspirations upon external paths. The Buddha does not permit the performance of the *poṣadha* with such externalists; if these persons do not abandon such views, they should not be permitted to participate in the affairs of the Saṃgha, nor should their *kāya* (consent) be accepted.

If, after being exhorted in this manner, he still does not relinquish [the offense], it should be known that this person cannot remain on the Path and is effectively abandoned; one should inform his Upādhyāya and Ācārya, and he should no longer be kept as a disciple.
Śāriputra! If the Saṃgha acts in this way, it honors me and effectively refutes the false views of the non-Buddhists; this is called the pure recitation of the precepts for the Poṣadha ceremony.
“Śāriputra! I now tell you clearly:

if a person holds these views—the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of existence and non-existence—that person cannot be said to be making offerings to me, nor can they be said to have left home and received the precepts following me. Such a person is called one who follows the six teachers and has taken those six teachers as their own masters.”
Śāriputra! If a person cannot attain patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) regarding this pure and true Dharma, yet accepts offerings, what that person receives is a perverted reception.

Śāriputra! Although such a person has left the household life within my Dharma and maintains pure precepts, they lack faith, understanding, and are struck with alarm, fear, doubt, and regret regarding the dharma of non-attainment in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). You should know that such a person merely prizes the observance of precepts, extensive learning, and meditative concentration.
Śāriputra! Such a person cannot be said to be making offerings to, honoring, or respecting me. Why is this?

Śāriputra! Since beginningless time, there has been no sentient being who has not attained the four dhyānas. If one merely knows how to attain the four dhyānas and considers that to be the benefit of a śramaṇa, how can such a person be said to be making an offering to me?
Therefore, Śāriputra, I now tell you clearly:
in future generations, there will be those within my Dharma who, through various attachments and various false views, shall destroy my Dharma.

“Śāriputra! If a person values only the observance of precepts, extensive learning, and meditative concentration, you should know that such a person cannot purify the various dharmas of a śramaṇa; I do not call such a person a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa.”

Śāriputra! If a person, regarding all phenomena as selfless, knows them as they truly are to be selfless; and regarding all phenomena as originally non-existent and empty, knows them as they truly are to be non-existent and empty—then such a person does not regard the observance of precepts as supreme, nor extensive learning as supreme, nor meditative concentration as supreme.
Why is this? Śāriputra, the true mark of all dharmas is without birth and without arising; therein, there is no dharma that can be considered superior.
Śāriputra! Within the suchness of these dharmas, there is no one who observes the precepts and no one who violates them; how much less could one be attached to them as being supreme?
Śāriputra! This is called the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi of all buddhas; it means that all dharmas are signless, empty of self-characteristic, and devoid of self or person.
If one possesses this patience, they are called a practitioner and are called an attainer.
Such a person is said to have left the household life through faith; they should receive offerings and the pure *poṣadha*, and they are truly a god among humans.
“Śāriputra! The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas has but a single meaning, which is detachment (*viveka*).
What is this detachment?
One is free from all desires and all views.
Desire is precisely ignorance; view is precisely recollection. Why is this so?
All dharmas have recollection as their basis; whatever thoughts and perceptions exist are themselves views, and such views are erroneous.
Śāriputra, even a view regarding wholesome dharmas—I also declare that to be called wrong view.
Why is this? Śāriputra!

Within the tranquility of detachment from desire, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither good nor evil; all these things are empty, far removed from all fetters and all recollections. For this reason, it is called "detachment."
Śāriputra! Within the unsurpassed path, all desires are forever stilled.
What are these desires?
This refers to wrong and unwholesome thoughts, such as "I" or "mine," and the signs of activity or objective characteristics.
This is called the eternal cessation of all desires within *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha-Store Sūtra, Middle Volume;
The Buddha-Store Sūtra, Lower Volume.
Translated by Kumārajīva, Tripiṭaka Master of Kucha during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On Pure Vision (Part Two) The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“I recall that in past ages, while seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I encountered thirty billion Buddhas, all of whom were named Śākyamuni.”

At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) in each instance and made offerings throughout my entire life—providing robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—to them and their disciples, all in order to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Yet these Buddhas did not bestow upon me the prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
For what reason?
"Because I had something to attain. "Śāriputra!
I recall that in past ages I encountered eight thousand Buddhas, all of whom were named Dīpaṃkara."

At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) in each instance, providing offerings throughout my entire life—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—to him and his disciples, all in order to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Yet none of those Buddhas predicted of me:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood.
For what reason?
"Because I had something to attain. "Śāriputra!
I recall that in past lives I encountered sixty thousand buddhas, all of whom were named Prabhāsa (Radiant Light)."

At that time, I became a Wheel-Turning Sage King in each instance and made offerings throughout my entire life—including robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—to him and his disciples, in order to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, those Buddhas did not grant me this prediction:
