"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood. Why is this?
"Because I had something to attain. "Śāriputra!
I recall that in past ages I encountered three hundred million Buddhas, all of whom were named Puṣya."
"At that time, I served as a universal monarch (cakravartin) and made offerings of the four requisites;
yet he did not grant me a prediction [of enlightenment], because I still harbored the notion of attainment. Śāriputra!"
I recall that in past lives I encountered eighteen thousand Buddhas, all of whom were named Mountain King, and the eon was called Superior Eight.
At the abodes of all these eighteen thousand Buddhas, I shaved my hair, donned the Dharma robes, and cultivated *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
yet none of them bestowed a prediction upon me, because I still held to the notion of attainment.
“Śāriputra! I recall that in past ages I encountered five hundred Buddhas, all of whom were named Puṣpadhvaja.
At that time, I was always a Cakravartin King and provided every kind of offering to those Buddhas and their disciples;”
"In all those cases, they did not grant me a prediction because I still harbored the notion of attainment. Śāriputra,
I recall that in past lives I encountered five hundred Buddhas, all of whom were named Wēidé (Majestic Virtue), and I made offerings to them all."
"In all those cases, they did not grant me a prediction because I still harbored the notion of attainment. Śāriputra,
I recall that in past lives I encountered two thousand Buddhas, all of whom were named Kauṇḍinya."
At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) in each instance and offered all manner of requisites to the Buddhas;
yet none of them bestowed a prediction upon me, because I still harbored the notion of attainment.
“Śāriputra! I recall that in past ages I encountered nine thousand Buddhas, all of whom were named Kāśyapa.
I made offerings of the four requisites to those Buddhas and their assemblies of disciples;”
"In all those cases, they did not grant me a prediction because I still harbored the notion of attainment.

Śāriputra, I recall that in the past, throughout ten thousand kalpas, no Buddha appeared. During the first five hundred kalpas of that period, there were ninety thousand pratyekabuddhas; for as long as I lived, I provided them all with offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, honoring and praising them."
For the next five hundred kalpas, he again made offerings of the four requisites to eighty-four trillion pratyekabuddhas, honoring and praising them. Śāriputra!
After these thousand kalpas had passed, there were no longer any pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, I died in Jambudvīpa and was reborn in the Brahma world as a Great Brahmā King. In this manner, throughout five hundred successive kalpas, I was constantly reborn in the Brahma world as a Great Brahmā King and was never born again in Jambudvīpa.

After these five hundred kalpas have passed, he will descend to be born in Jambudvīpa; there he will govern and transform Jambudvīpa, and at the end of his life, he will be reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings. There, at the end of his life, he will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, becoming Śakra Devendra.
In this manner, he passed through five hundred kalpas in succession, was born in Jambudvīpa for five hundred kalpas, and was born in the Brahma world to become a Great Brahmā King. “Śāriputra!

Throughout nine thousand kalpas, I was born only once in Jambudvīpa; for those nine thousand kalpas, I was born only in the heavens. When the kalpas ended and were consumed by fire, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; when the world was reconstituted, I returned to the Brahma-world. Throughout those nine thousand kalpas, I was never born among human beings.
“Śāriputra! During these nine thousand kalpas, there will be no Buddhas or pratyekabuddhas, and many sentient beings will fall into the evil realms. Śāriputra!”

After ten thousand kalpas had passed, a Buddha appeared in the world, named Pǔshǒu (Universal Protector) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
At that time, having passed away from the Brahma world, I was reborn in Jambudvīpa as a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Sahadeva.
The lifespan of humans was ninety thousand years.

For as long as my life lasted, I provided all manner of requisites for pleasure to that Buddha and nine hundred million bhikṣus; for ninety thousand years, I sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet that Buddha Viśvārakṣita did not say to me:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha."
Why is this? At that time, I was unable to penetrate the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas), for I was greedily attached to the view of a self and the notion of having something attained.
"Śāriputra!..."
In that kalpa, one hundred Buddhas appeared, each with a different name and title.

At that time, I was in every instance a Cakravartin King, making offerings throughout my entire life to those Buddhas and their disciples, seeking Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; yet these Buddhas did not grant me the prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha."
"Because they held to the notion of attainment.
Śāriputra, I recall that in the past,
during the seventh incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) ago, I encountered a thousand Buddhas, all of whom were named Jambūnada."
"I served them with the four requisites for as long as I lived, yet they did not grant me a prediction because I still harbored the notion of attainment.
Śāriputra, I recall that in a past life, during the seventh asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I encountered six million two hundred thousand Buddhas, all of whom were named Sarvārthadarśin."
At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) and provided all manner of articles of pleasure as offerings to him and his disciples for the duration of my life;
yet he did not grant me a prediction [of enlightenment], because I still harbored the notion of attainment.
“Śāriputra! I recall that in a past life, during the seventh asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I encountered eighty-four Buddhas, all of whom were named Tiexiang (Imperial Mark).”
At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) and, with all articles of pleasure, made offerings to him and his disciples for as long as I lived;
yet he did not grant me a prediction [of enlightenment], because I still harbored the notion of attainment.
“Śāriputra! I recall that in a past life, during the seventh incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), I encountered sixty-five Buddhas, all of whom were named Sūryaprabha (Sunlight).”
At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) and provided all manner of articles of enjoyment to him and his disciples for as long as I lived;
yet he did not grant me a prediction [of enlightenment], because I still possessed the notion of attainment.
“Śāriputra! I recall that in the past, during the seventh asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I encountered sixty-two Buddhas, all of whom were named Śānta.”
At that time, I became a universal monarch (cakravartin) and provided offerings of every kind of pleasure throughout my entire life;
yet he did not grant me a prediction [of enlightenment], because I still harbored the notion of attainment.
Thus, passing through successive stages until I beheld Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).

He then bestowed upon me this prophecy: "In a future age, after incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
“Śāriputra! I recall that in a past age there were twelve hundred million wheel-turning sage-kings, all named Mūrdhaja.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
In past ages, there were thirty billion wheel-turning sage-kings, all named Mahānamadhana. Śāriputra,
I recall that in past ages there were forty billion wheel-turning sage-kings, all named Mahādeva.
Śāriputra! I recall that in a past age there were one hundred million wheel-turning sage kings, all of whom were named Aruṇa (億螺). Śāriputra!
I recall that in a past age there were one hundred million wheel-turning sage-kings, all of whom were named Vemacitra.
Śāriputra! I recall that in a past age there were ten thousand wheel-turning sage-kings, all of whom were named Jyotiṣprabha.
Śāriputra! I recall that in past ages there were twenty thousand wheel-turning sage-kings, each with a different name. Śāriputra!
I recall that in past ages there were sixteen hundred million wheel-turning sage-kings, each with a different name; I have spoken of these kings to Ānanda on other occasions.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Do you suppose that these various kings were anyone other than [the ones you have heard of]?
"I am that very person. Śāriputra,
I recall that in a past age there was a Buddha named Sunlight (Suvimalaprabha)."
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Jiaoming (Illumination), who first gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the lifespan of sentient beings was eighty-four thousand years.
That Buddha, Śubhaprabha, preached the Dharma on three occasions. At the first assembly, ninety-six billion people simultaneously attained the Way;
at the second great assembly, ninety-four billion people simultaneously attained the Way;
and at the third great assembly, ninety-two billion people simultaneously attained the Way.

At that time, the king saw the Buddha preach the Dharma in three assemblies, delivering immeasurable numbers of people. His heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately provided all manner of offerings to the Buddha and his disciples for ten thousand years. He then resolved to seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, vowing:
"In a future age, when sentient beings are easy to deliver, I shall become a Buddha; my lifespan shall be of such measure, and I shall be surrounded by a community of bhikṣus of such number."
“Śāriputra! I know that this matter exceeds even this by immeasurable degrees. Śāriputra!”
Forty kalpas after Maitreya first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], I then resolved my mind.

Under the Buddha Anabhibhū, I first planted roots of goodness; for a thousand years, I made offerings to that Buddha with every kind of delightful requisite, presenting him with five hundred pieces of fine cloth.

After this Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a stūpa made of the seven precious substances will be erected, one yojana in height and half a yojana in length and breadth, entirely composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, and red pearls.
One should constantly make this vow:

"When sentient beings suffer in affliction without anyone to deliver them, and when they encounter evil dharmas and mostly fall into the evil realms—at that time, I shall attain the Way of the Buddha."
“Śāriputra! You should observe this: Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is extremely difficult to cultivate. Śāriputra!”

I have cultivated *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and endured various sufferings and afflictions throughout incalculable eons; if I were to speak of them, you would become distressed upon hearing it. All the diligent hardships and anxieties I have undergone were solely for the sake of seeking to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra! Observe the Bodhisattva Sahadatta, the Bodhisattva Seeking the Good Dharma, the Bodhisattva Constant Compassion, the Bodhisattva Heedfulness, and the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence; even though they made offerings to numerous Buddhas and underwent various sufferings and afflictions, it was still difficult for them to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. How much more so for these deluded people, who do not have a single thought of seeking nirvāṇa?
"Śāriputra! Even for one who practices in this way, it is still exceedingly difficult; how much more so for one who does not practice?
Therefore, Śāriputra!"
I now declare this clearly to you: those who employ inferior methods do not attain superior methods; only those who employ superior methods attain superior methods.
What are the inferior methods?
These refer to evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind.
Inferior qualities are defined as being unable to diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas with the mind;
inferior qualities are defined as indolence, laziness, and the breaking of the precepts one has undertaken.
Śāriputra! This is called the lowest of the middle-low.

Furthermore, as for the lowest of the middle-low, they leave the household life within my Dharma, yet give rise to views of attainment, views of a self, views of a person, and views of sentient beings.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata clearly perceives and knows that those who have any attainment whatsoever lack even the patience of compliance (anulomikī-kṣānti), let alone the fruit of the Path.

Śāriputra! If there is one who clings to attainment, even if hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas were to manifest before that person through the three wheels of action, if they do not abandon this view, they will not even digest a single mouthful of food offered by others, let alone attain the fruits of the Path.
“Śāriputra! If those with the view of a self and the view of a person were to attain nirvāṇa, then all ordinary worldlings should have already been delivered. Why is this?
The view of a self and the view of a person are both false views.
Ordinary worldlings are mostly greedily attached to the view of "I" and "mine," the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being.
"Therefore, all ordinary persons should attain nirvana. Śāriputra,
if a person who conceives of a self and a person were to enter nirvana without abandoning such views, then all ordinary persons should attain the noble path."
Why is this? All ordinary beings possess the view of self and the view of a person.
Therefore, if those with the view of self and the view of a person were to enter nirvāṇa, all ordinary beings would enter the noble path, and within that noble path, there would be nothing lacking.
“Śāriputra! If a person harbors the thought that there is a self-view, then for them there is nirvāṇa; such a person attains this noble path without needing further reflection. Why is this?
Because all ordinary persons lack nothing in terms of the view of self and the view of a person.
Such is the fault of these deluded people: they claim that all ordinary persons enter the noble path, and that the noble path is unconditioned.
When such a person practices, they should take life, indulge in the five desires, and commit the five heinous crimes.
Therefore, this deluded person incurs the five heinous crimes within the Noble Path.
Why is this? Because all ordinary worldlings claim that there is a self and there are sentient beings.
If someone were to speak in this way:

"To say, 'One who has committed the five heinous crimes does not enter nirvana, whereas one who speaks of a self and a person attains nirvana,' is both a falsehood and a slander of the Buddha; such a person cannot attain pure renunciation within my Dharma."
“Śāriputra! I now tell you clearly: for those who have something to attain, there is no nirvāṇa.
If those who have something to attain were to enter nirvāṇa, then the Buddhas would not appear in the world, and all ordinary beings would already have entered nirvāṇa.”
Why is this? All ordinary persons possess the view of a self and the view of a person; all who hold to attainment possess false views.
"Śāriputra!..."

"You should observe me: for how long have I maintained the view of something to be attained and engaged in practices that are not those of the noble ones, such that the Buddhas did not grant me the prediction, saying, 'In a future age, you shall become a Buddha'?"
"Śāriputra! Even though I practice in this way, I have still not received a prediction;

how much less so for these deluded people who, by means of mere observance of precepts, extensive learning, and meditative concentration, give rise to the view of a self, the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being?"
Śāriputra! I say that such a person is not called a practitioner, nor is he called one who has attained. Why is this?
Śāriputra! Because they have been greedily attached to such false views throughout the long night, they do not attain extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
Such deluded people do not form this thought:
"Shāriputra! Why do we not try to practice and cultivate the non-existence of self and of persons or dharmas?
Perhaps we may attain the severance of this entire mass of suffering. Shāriputra!
Śāriputra, it is as if a man born blind, fleeing from a vicious dog, were to fall into a deep pit of fire.

I say that such foolish people cultivate the view of a self, the view of a person, and the view of attaining something; yet, with these various views, they desire purity. Following their own attachments, they seek to attain nirvāṇa through those very things.
"I say that such a person shall fall into the evil realms.

Śāriputra, it is as if a blind man were to feel a sense of security while standing at the edge of a deep fire-pit; likewise, these deluded people feel a sense of security in their views of self and personhood, and in the view that there is something to be attained. For a long night, such people follow after that to which they are attached and are deceived by it, remaining attached to those very things even while receiving offerings within my Dharma. Thus, these deluded people suffer decline and affliction for a long night and fall into the evil realms."
“Śāriputra! It is like a great anointed king who, within the realm over which he rules, possesses sovereign power and authority, such that he may seize some persons and banish others.”

If there are subjects who do not obey the king’s will, who speak of the king’s faults and evils to undermine the people's hearts, and who cannot protect the city but plot rebellion—the king, knowing these individuals to be great thieves, beats the drum of ill omen amidst the great assembly, inflicts severe punishment upon them, and banishes them. Because they were unable to remain loyal and protect the city, they undergo such suffering and distress.

Śāriputra! The Buddha is also like this: having cultivated *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for immeasurable eons, he has become a Great Dharma King who possesses great sovereign power over his dharma-realm.

Among my disciples, there are those who have realized the flavor of the Dharma; even at the cost of their lives, they do not disparage my teaching, and no gods or worldly beings can subvert it. Within the teachings they have received, they themselves do not act with malice or rebellion, nor do they incite others to do so.

Within this assembly, I possess great power and authority; I shall establish the teaching as a citadel for protecting the Dharma, so that wicked thieves may not enter and destroy it, nor steal the secret teachings spoken by the Tathāgata to preach them to enemies, bandits, and those of wrong views.

“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata currently guards the city of the Dharma well; as the four great disciples possess profound and far-reaching wisdom, my city of the Dharma now has no fear of being destroyed.”
If one creates obstacles for the City of Dharma, such a person is a great thief who destroys the City of Dharma and steals my secret teachings to proclaim them to those of external paths.
Such a person constantly comes to me; I converse with them and show them the general teachings, but I do not speak of the essential secrets.

This person has left the household life and received the precepts in order to seek the teachings shown; I know that this person shall later attain the Way, so I permit him to leave the household life and test him for four months.
Why is this? It is for the sake of protecting the city of the Dharma, and so that thieves in future ages may not arise again.

In this way, the Tathāgata skillfully protects the city of the Dharma so that they find no opportunity; that is to say, he causes them to receive the Buddha’s teaching and abandon their original evil heterodoxy. All the community of bhikṣus should rejoice, and having permitted them to go forth and receive the precepts, neither gods, humans, nor the world can cause them to waver.
“Śāriputra, who are those who may be tested?
They are the followers of external paths and those who delight in the teachings of external paths.”
Śāriputra! What is it to delight in the teachings of external paths?

It refers to those who hold to the notion of attainment, those with the view of a self, those with the view of a person, those with the view of a sentient being, those who are greedy, those who are heterodox, and those whose minds harbor doubt regarding the dharmas that are empty of intrinsic characteristics. They accept and practice various kinds of heterodox and false teachings, unable to enter the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and they follow various wrong paths; such persons are said to delight in the teachings of external paths.
“Śāriputra! One must not test them with robes of various colors.
Whether they be laypeople wearing white garments or those wearing the kāṣāya, if they possess such unwholesome views of attainment, they are all called non-Buddhists (tīrthika).”
Those who have left the household life and received the precepts within my Dharma should undergo examination. Why is this?
For one who holds to anything as attainable within my Dharma possesses a false view; such a person is called a great thief.
They are thieves among all the worlds of devas and humans; they are called enemies of all the worlds and great thieves of the Buddhas.
Śāriputra, I do not permit such people of false views to leave the household life or receive the precepts.

“Śāriputra! All dharmas are without self. If a person cannot give rise to patience toward this, and cannot believe or understand that all dharmas are empty, without self, without a person, without a sentient being, and without a life-span, then the offerings they receive within my Dharma are called impure.”
Such a person does not make offerings to the Buddha, does not make offerings to the Dharma, and does not make offerings to the Saṅgha.
Though they have forcibly entered my Dharma, their form is that of a śramaṇa while their mind is that of a non-Buddhist; they are a thief of the Dharma.
“Śāriputra! In a future age, there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate ethical discipline, do not cultivate the mind, and do not cultivate wisdom.”
Such people laugh at what the Tathāgata has taught and what the Tathāgata has practiced.
The Tathāgata always dwells in the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and he constantly reveres, makes offerings to, and delights in this practice.
These bhikṣus derided and laughed at the Tathāgata’s practice of the ultimate reality—the dharma of absolute emptiness. Śāriputra!

At that time, if there were any bhikṣus practicing austerities, they too would have joined in this derision. (Now, among my disciples, those who practice emptiness—I praise their goodness and comfort their minds.)

At that time, such a person despises the practice of emptiness and seeks only those things that are not firm; by asserting the existence of a self and the existence of various phenomena, they cause the minds of the multitude to rejoice.
If one says that all dharmas are empty, one likewise disparages such a person.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Such is the nature of phenomena.

When the roots of goodness of sentient beings are about to be severed, their original characteristics manifest; though the true and wondrous Dharma remains in the world, there is no one to receive it.
It is like a foolish person who treats sandalwood as equal to common, low-grade wood.
"Śāriputra! Kāśyapa Buddha said: [that those who disparage this teaching are like such fools]."
"In a future age, the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, for the sake of gain and offerings, will preach the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) to laypeople."

At that time, there will be many householders and renunciants who, being ignorant, will not accept [the teaching], will oppose it, and will lack faith; instead, they will slander it and thereby lose great benefit.
Because of these causes and conditions, they shall fall into the evil realms.”

“Śāriputra! At that time, there will be many conflicting disputes: theories of a self, theories of a person, theories of a sentient being, theories of a life-force, and theories of a vital principle. With little desire for wholesome dharmas, they will take pleasure only in gain and offerings; being truly foolish yet claiming to possess wisdom, they will oppose one another and constantly engage in litigation, delighting in legal proceedings and giving rise to hearts of enmity and jealousy.”

Such a person abandons the dharma of a śramaṇa and seeks only gain and offerings; they take great pleasure in many affairs and have numerous undertakings; they constantly delight in seeking out the faults of others while concealing their own transgressions and proclaiming their own virtues (just as bhikṣus today conceal their virtues and openly display their faults).
At that time, they were all unable to maintain the heavy precepts; because they lacked understanding, they violated the ritual rules and said:
"All phenomena are empty, their own characteristics are empty; what can they possibly do?"
"Just as when a Nara-actor performs various transformations, those who lack understanding see them and laugh loudly.
Why is this? Because they do not know the art of the performance and its techniques remain hidden, they conceive a sense of wonder and, being struck with astonishment, laugh loudly."
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
At that time, when a bhikṣu of true reality preached the Dharma of emptiness and stillness, those who sought their livelihood all mocked him together. Why was this?
Because these people do not understand the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, they are startled, doubtful, and terrified upon hearing the teaching of emptiness.
Śāriputra, observe these people:

they conceive thoughts of decline and affliction regarding that which is secure, and they conceive thoughts of security regarding that which leads to decline and affliction. These people act perversely and contrary to wholesome dharmas, while acting in accordance with unwholesome dharmas.
"Śāriputra!
Such deluded people harbor much stinginess, greed, anger, and folly, fully practicing the three unwholesome roots. Śāriputra!"
For the sake of benefiting those bhikṣus who uphold the precepts, I have taught the Sūtra of Two Hundred and Fifty Precepts.
Yet such deluded persons, on account of some trivial worldly circumstance, speak of them to laypeople, even going so far as to write them down and show them to householders.
Śāriputra! Such deluded people say: "All phenomena are empty;
they are empty of their own characteristics. What can they possibly do?"
Why is this? Such deluded people are unable to even eliminate the afflictions of stinginess and greed, let alone sever ignorance. “Śāriputra!
At that time, the bhikṣus who maintained the Vinaya could not study it well; those who preached the Dharma likewise could not study it well, nor could those who recited the Sūtras study them well.
Śāriputra! What is meant by a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya being unable to train well?
In the sūtras, the Tathāgata has taught that there are three trainings:
The training in virtuous precepts, the training in virtuous mind, and the training in virtuous wisdom.
If a person cannot train well in these three trainings, but instead, by virtue of their extensive learning, treats others with contempt, that person creates an obstacle to wholesome dharmas.
Such a deluded person is unable even to answer a question in accordance with the Dharma, let alone be able to exert diligence within ultimate emptiness where nothing exists.
"Śāriputra!..."
At that time, monks who have broken the precepts will delight in performing services for laypeople, acting as messengers, and practicing medical treatments to sustain their livelihoods. Śāriputra!
"Observe now, Śāriputra, this evil person who has gone forth and received the precepts within my Dharma, yet having obtained offerings, has instead treated me as an enemy."

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra-devānām-indra, Mahābrahmā, and even hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of devas, seeing such destruction within my Dharma, were all filled with great sorrow and wept with falling tears.
Śāriputra! This truly ought not to be done; one should not rely upon me to manage affairs for laypeople. Why is this?

Even the disciples of Śākyamuni Buddha, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, should not serve as attendants; rather, it is the devas, nāgas, and spirits who shall serve as attendants to my disciples.
"It is impossible, Śāriputra, that such a deluded person who associates with laypeople could cultivate and penetrate the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena."
At that time, a precept-breaking bhikṣu might even preach the Buddha-dharma to laypeople for the sake of obtaining a single cup of wine.
What do you think?

If one has much greed, anger, and delusion, yet delights greatly in reciting scriptures, and while craving the benefits of external teachings, their conduct is not pure—can such a person attain faith and understanding of the dharma of non-existence and ultimate emptiness? Can they attain the fruits of the śramaṇa in their full perfection?
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"

If there is a bhikṣu who obtains robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine with ease; who maintains pure precepts; who does not delight in the clamor of crowds or in distracted speech; who does not crave external doctrines but practices with diligence day and night as if his head were on fire; and who single-mindedly and diligently cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path.

If even such a person finds it difficult to penetrate the dharma of non-attainment in emptiness, how much more so for this deluded person, who lacks profound aspiration and lacks faith and understanding? Śāriputra!

Observe this person: because they do not understand the unsurpassed meaning of the Tathāgata, they destroy my True Dharma. They bring about great ruin and affliction for themselves and for others. Such a great thief and enemy of the world should be shunned, as stated in this sutra.
Such persons do not even recognize the Buddha's kindness, thinking to themselves:
"For what purpose have we gone forth?
Within this Dharma, we must not engage in those things that are improper to practice."
"Therefore, Śāriputra, because the Tathāgata wishes to cause this evil to cease in future ages, he has preached such a sūtra as this.

If there are bhikṣus who have broken the precepts they received, violated their dignified conduct, or corrupted their right view, upon hearing this sūtra, they will become terrified and return to the precepts."
Why is this? A person who has broken the precepts should not, even for the duration of a finger-snap, abide in the appearance of a noble one while wearing the kāṣāya.
If one hears this sutra and their heart rejoices, such a person is said to be making offerings to all Buddhas and guarding the Buddha-way.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
this is called the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of the Buddha-way.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to attain the qualities of a śramaṇa, they should travel across hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yojanas to hear this sūtra. Why is this?
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world only after a long time; though they have appeared in the world, they speak of this only at such a time.
Chapter Nine: On the Fulfillment of the Precepts (Lower) *The Sūtra of the Buddha-Treasury*, Chapter Nine: On the Fulfillment of the Precepts. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“There are three kinds of people who, upon hearing this sūtra being preached, do not find joy or delight in their hearts.”
What are the three?
First, bhikṣus who violate the precepts;
second, those with overweening pride; [and third, those who have not yet attained realization].
Third, those who preach the Dharma impurely and are greedily attached to a self.
Such people distance themselves from these profound sūtras that accord with the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and are fully comprised within the class of those born blind.
Therefore, Śāriputra,
I entrust this sutra to you with special emphasis. Why is this?
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, this sutra will be able to bring joy and delight to the hearts of bhikṣus who maintain pure precepts.
Such a profound sutra as this is always upheld by those of pure morality, while it is always shunned by those who have violated their precepts.
Why is this? When foolish people hear the true and correct words being spoken, they regard them as suffering. "Śāriputra!
The characteristics possessed by a precept-breaking bhikṣu have already been explained in detail by the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra, it is the nature of a precept-breaking bhikṣu not to delight in maintaining the discipline of the precepts; such a foolish person takes no pleasure in wisdom.
The miserly do not wish to hear the teaching on giving;
those with overweening pride do not wish to hear this Dharma that is free from arrogance, for if they hear it, they are struck with terror as if falling into a deep pit;
and those who crave worldly gain are attached to fine flavors, so when they hear food disparaged, their minds become distressed.
If a person delights in reading external scriptures, they will conceive of them as being solid and substantial;
those who crave words take pleasure in discursive speech and delight in ornate rhetoric;
and those skilled in elegant eloquence lack a pure mind regarding the Buddha’s ultimate truth, and furthermore, they harbor neither reverence nor faith toward this Dharma.
Śāriputra! It is as if a eunuch, lacking the functions of a man, were to perceive those among men as being eunuchs and think to himself:
"These people are no different from me."

"In this way, those who are fondly attached to external scriptures always delight in elaborate adornment and artful, flowery rhetoric, and their minds lack reverence for the Buddha’s primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Śāriputra!"

Among them, some may preach the Sūtras of Purity, yet they do not show respect toward such persons, but instead treat with contempt and disdain those bhikṣus who maintain purity and uphold the precepts. Why is this?
Śāriputra! The scriptures of the non-Buddhists contain no words of truth; their nature is one of arrogance, conceit, and self-importance. Why is this?

This matter does not lead to wearying detachment, nor to tranquility, nor to the attainment of the Path, nor to Nirvana; because such a person has destroyed their roots of goodness such as faith, they do not believe in the existence of merit in any place, just as a eunuch regards all among men as being like himself.
“Śāriputra! It is like a person born blind who does not see various forms—namely, black and white; one who does not see black or white; who does not see beautiful colors or ugly colors;

who does not see blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, or azure; who does not see long, short, coarse, fine, deep, or shallow colors; and who does not see the sun, moon, or stars—one who does not see the sun, moon, or stars.”
Then that blind man thought to himself:

"There are no black or white colors, nor anyone who sees black or white; there are no beautiful or ugly forms, nor blue, yellow, purple, or pale green; there are no long or short, coarse or fine, deep or shallow, nor the colors of the sun, moon, and stars, nor anyone who sees the sun, moon, and stars; all other people are exactly like this!"
"The blind man’s mind is inverted, such that he perceives everything as darkness.

Śāriputra, it is the same with bhikṣus who have broken their precepts, those of overweening pride, and bhikṣus who have fallen into the doctrines of external paths: they lack faith and delight in the profound Buddha-dharma and cannot penetrate it; hearing that all dharmas are empty and non-existent, they do not believe or delight in them and cannot penetrate them."

Śāriputra! Such people as these fear you and others; they enter into a state of deviation and fail to attain the True Dharma. It is for this reason that the True Dharma is called the "genuine śramaṇa."
Others will not believe the Dharma you have attained, just as a blind person claims that colors such as white and black do not exist.

Śāriputra, such people enter into the extreme of error; they seek out the treatises of non-Buddhists and delight in worldly clamor, thereby increasing their afflictions, evil dispositions, and unwholesome dharmas. These people cannot even believe in the emptiness of all phenomena, let alone realize it.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Can a jackal, acting as a lion, roar in the past, roar now, or roar in the future; or can it perform the conduct of a lion, perform it now, perform it in the future, or have performed it in the past?
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
The jackal’s physical strength and voice do not equal those of the lion; the jackal can only produce the sound of a jackal.
If it wishes to make a sound, only the sound of a jackal emerges, not the sound of a lion.

“In this way, Śāriputra, a precept-breaking bhikṣu and a bhikṣu of overweening pride consider such matters to be supreme; those who preach the Dharma impurely accept the treatises of the Nirgranthas; if they cling to a single point, holding fast to it without relinquishing it, and greedily prize worldly gain while delighting in reading scriptures, they will be unable to penetrate the true mark of all dharmas.”
"It is impossible for one who can believe and accept the dharma of signlessness to exist [in this world]. Śāriputra!

If there is a bhikṣu of advanced age and great virtue, a dragon among bhikṣus possessing profound wisdom, such a person is able to believe in the dharma of non-existence, the emptiness of self-characteristics, and the absence of self and persons."
Why is this? Because such a person does not delight in the clamor and idle chatter of crowds;
nor do they delight in reciting scriptures, sleeping, or being preoccupied with many affairs.
They do not engage in administrative affairs on behalf of laypeople;
they do not act as messengers to carry documents;
they do not practice medicine, nor study medical prescriptions, nor engage in trade, nor delight in discussing worldly talk, but rather delight only in speaking of supramundane matters.
This person is able to believe that all phenomena are empty, and thus neither gives rise to nor destroys any phenomenon.
This person is then able to realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and can truly roar the lion’s roar according to reality, not the jackal’s howl.

“Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who clings to the doctrines of external scriptures, such a person abandons the subtle and wondrous Buddha-dharma; reciting and upholding the words of non-Buddhists to preach to the great assembly, he merely makes the howl of a jackal.”
Śāriputra! Such evil persons are called "rotten śramaṇas. Why is this?
This is the doctrine of the non-Buddhists, not that of the Buddha-dharma. "Śāriputra,
a bhikṣu who clings to the teachings of the non-Buddhists should not claim to be a disciple of the Buddha."
Why is this? The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not speak the words of the Nirgranthas; in the midst of the great assembly, they speak only the words of the Buddha. Śāriputra!
If a person, while clinging to impure speech, wishes to let out a lion’s roar, they will merely utter the cry of a jackal; such a person cannot understand the primary meaning of the Buddha-dharma.

“Śāriputra! I now tell you clearly: if a person fully maintains the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom; is neither stingy nor greedy; is untainted by anger or delusion; harbors no deceit or crookedness but possesses a mind of renunciation; speaks only what is true; always delights in solitude and does not delight in sleep; rejoices in the practices of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, non-arising, and non-ceasing; gives rise to a mind detached from desire to seek the ultimate truth of the Buddha-dharma; does not favor worldly talk but delights in supramundane talk; and fully upholds all the precepts while remaining far removed from all evil deeds and evil associates—then by abiding in such dharmas, one will be able to understand the dharma of emptiness and non-existence.”
Why is this? Śāriputra,
this practice is called that which is practiced by great beings.

This is not the conduct of those who crave gain and offerings; it is not the conduct of foolish ordinary people; it is not the conduct of degenerate śramaṇas; it is not the conduct of śramaṇas who are like dregs; it is not the conduct of śramaṇas who are merely nominal.

“Śāriputra! The true mark of all dharmas is ultimately empty and quiescent; this is itself the Buddha-way, which those who delight in worldly wealth and profit and preach impure dharmas cannot attain.”
Śāriputra! This stage is called the stage of those with great wisdom;
it is not the stage of those who delight in external paths, nor is it the stage of those who propound the view of a self or the view of a person.
“Śāriputra! If there were truly a self or a person, and if those who speak of a self or a person were to exist as such, they would have to possess a real characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
Accordingly, one should ask as follows:”
"If there were a self, what would its color be?
Blue, yellow, red, or white?
Would it be within the body?"
"Is it outside the body?
Or does it pervade the entire body, like oil within sesame seeds?
"Śāriputra! [the Buddha said.]
There is oil within the hemp; it can be extracted and demonstrated.
If I were within [the body] and claimed that there was a self, I should be able to speak of it and demonstrate it, just as one extracts oil from hemp and shows the oil.

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), a self cannot be found; therefore, you should know that if one speaks of the existence of a self or a person (*pudgala*), such a person does not even possess the precepts of a śramaṇa, let alone the stage of a śramaṇa.
“Śāriputra, you should know that such wrong attachments— namely, attachment to a self, attachment to sentient beings, and attachment to a life-span— are what constitute falling from the summit.”
Because such a person is thus perversely attached, they are unable to eliminate even the mind that craves gain and offerings, let alone subtle afflictions.

Śāriputra, it is impossible for one who has attained penetration of emptiness to be overwhelmed by greed, anger, delusion, or the pursuit of gain and offerings; nor would such a person fall from the summit [of the path].
“Śāriputra! Those who calculate my mind as having a life-span, because of that life-span as a causal condition, will be led astray by gain and offerings, thereby obstructing the Path.”

Śāriputra! Those who hold the view of a self or the view of a person, though they have left the household life to practice the Way within my Dharma, such deluded people are not truly renunciants within the state of purity.
Why is this? Because the Nirgrantha-putras who have left the household life all reckon that there is something to be gained within their own minds. Śāriputra!

Those who hold to the view that there is something to be attained have always maintained this perspective since beginningless time; even if they leave the household life, this view remains unextinguished. This is called leaving the household life due to external paths, and is not called leaving the household life due to the Noble Dharma.
Why is this? Because base people cannot believe in or delight in the Great Dharma, and they lack a sense of its true reality regarding the pure Great Dharma. "Śāriputra!

Because the remaining retribution for the causes and conditions of such grave offenses of destroying the Dharma has not yet been exhausted, they are unable to believe in or understand the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. They give rise to unwholesome karma, either by slandering the Eightfold Noble Path;
or by conceiving evil thoughts toward bhikṣus of pure precepts and falsely proclaiming their faults;
or by saying that they have broken the precepts, broken the right view, broken their livelihood, or broken their dignified conduct.
Or they may falsely give rise to notions of right and wrong by not seeing the faults of others;
or they may speak ill of others with minds clouded by anger and envy;
or they may fail to understand the principles of the Buddha’s scriptures and claim them to be non-Buddhist teachings.
Such evil persons, having accomplished the evil karma of destroying the Dharma, do not penetrate, enter, or rejoice in the Buddha’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Due to the causal conditions of this heavy offense as its residual retribution, even though they exert themselves with diligence, they are still unable to grasp the characteristics of their objects of focus; how much less could they, by binding the mind, attain the fruits of the Path?
Furthermore, those who deeply rely upon the view of self and the view of a person—such views that even the Buddhas cannot uproot from their very foundation, let alone the śrāvakas.

“Śāriputra! If there are people who possess such unwholesome attachments and false views—namely, the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a life-principle—and who are startled, doubtful, and terrified by the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), you should know that these people have accomplished the karmic conditions for the sin of destroying the Dharma in their previous lives.”
Śāriputra!

If there are people who thus greedily cling to evil, heterodox, and unwholesome views—namely, those who crave a self, crave a person, or crave a life-span—even if hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas were to manifest before them through the three wheels of action, they could not cause such people to awaken and attain the fruit of the Path.

Śāriputra! It would be better to cut out one's tongue with a sharp blade than, failing to see another's actual faults, to falsely speak of their transgressions—whether regarding their violation of the precepts, their wrong views, their livelihood, or their deportment.
“Śāriputra! In a future age, there will be bhikṣus who well protect the two hundred and fifty precepts, yet conceit will arise in them and they will think:
‘I am one who upholds the precepts; others are not so!’”
They treat others with contempt, harboring no respect in their hearts, thinking:
"I am learned, while they are not learned. Śāriputra!

At that time, there were many bhikṣus who valued the observance of the precepts and practiced extensively in the forest hermitages (āraṇya). They were able to skillfully protect the categories of the precepts and act according to what was taught; with diligent minds, they recited the sūtras and sought to master the Buddha-dharma.

Such people as these give rise to pride in their learning and pride in their practice in the forest; they delight in anger, their minds are constantly defiled and turbid, and they harbor deep stinginess and greed. Possessing the poisonous mind of hatred, they are stubborn, dull-witted, and ignorant, giving rise to great calamities from minor causes.

These people, their minds shrouded by anger, will mutually expose each other's faults—namely, violations of the precepts, violations of right view, violations of livelihood, and violations of dignified conduct.

Śāriputra, within such a Saṃgha there may be virtuous bhikṣus who, being free from partiality, remain impartial; yet they too will be drawn into those evils, engaging in mutual derision, debate, and litigation without ceasing. Consequently, they will be unable to dwell in peace while practicing meditation or reciting the sūtras, and both laypeople and monastics alike will be disturbed.
“In this way, Śāriputra!

At that time, there will be many bhikṣus—one year, two years, three years, or even up to nine years in seniority—who treat their elders with contempt and lack reverence. These people, having left the household life and received the precepts, will for the most part act contrary to the Dharma; they will emulate their upādhyāyas and ācāryas, yet remain devoid of respect.”

Śāriputra! At that time, the young bhikṣus and those who had previously left the home life without a preceptor will mutually disparage the disciples maintained by bhikṣus of ten years' standing; those disciples will all lack reverence, proper deportment, and the rules of discipline, nor will they act in accordance with the Dharma.

Śāriputra! At that time, all those evil people will be fully possessed of greed, hatred, and delusion; they will treat one another with contempt and lack any sense of reverence. Because they act in mutual opposition, my Dharma will then perish.

“Śāriputra! At that time, many foolish people will frequently give rise to the karmic offenses of destroying the Dharma; having committed these offenses, they shall fall into the evil realms. Śāriputra!”
I now clearly inform you: a bhikṣu who seeks his own benefit and welfare should not enter a community for even a single night at such a time;
this applies with the sole exception of arhats whose afflictions have been severed, and sick bhikṣus who have a specific reason for being there.
Why is this? Śāriputra, at that time,
people will have the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion flourishing, and they will be constantly oppressed by the fear of being unable to survive.
Those seeking profit and virtue should always dwell in mountain forests and empty, quiet places, remaining there until the end of their lives, dying like wild beasts.
"Śāriputra! I now tell you clearly: this True Dharma of mine will not remain long in the world."

Why is this? Because the merit and roots of goodness of sentient beings have already been exhausted, and the age of turbidity is drawing near; a bhikṣu seeking his own benefit and virtue should give rise to such a sense of weary detachment, thinking: "What shall I do?"

"Seeing the disorder and turmoil of the Dharma, and seeing that this śramaṇa lives in an evil age of hardship, I shall apply myself with diligent mind and vigor to quickly attain the fruits of the Path.
"Śāriputra! [he said.]

In my Dharma there are no difficulties; do not concern yourselves with clothing, food, bedding, or medicine. You should simply apply yourselves diligently to the Buddha-way, and do not prize worldly wealth, profit, or offerings.
Śāriputra! Listen well now;
I shall speak to you.

Śāriputra, if there is a bhikṣu who practices the Path with a single-minded focus, ten billion celestial beings will all align their hearts and desire to collectively make offerings to him with every kind of musical instrument and requisite for pleasure. Śāriputra!
The offerings made by people do not equal those made by celestial beings.
Therefore, Śāriputra,
do not worry that you will not be able to provide for yourself.
The Buddha’s true teaching should be practiced in accordance with it; do not use the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) to expose the faults and evils of others.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
The great peril is what is called the attainment of emptiness.
There may be a bhikṣu who, having gone forth and received the precepts through my Dharma, practices with diligent vigor within this Dharma.

Although neither the various devas nor other people may think of them, those who are able to practice the Path with single-minded diligence will ultimately have no concern for the necessities of food and clothing. Why is this?
"The merit-treasury of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and inexhaustible. Śāriputra,

after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, if one were to divide the light from his ūrṇā-kośa into hundreds of thousands of billions of parts, and were to use even a single part of it to make offerings to the śarīras and all the disciples."

Śāriputra! Even if all the people in every world were to renounce the household life together and practice in accordance with the Dharma, they would not equal even one part in a hundred thousand billion parts of the white tuft between the eyebrows.
Śāriputra! Such are the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits that whatever food and drink the bhikṣus obtain, as well as whatever requisites they require, shall be sufficient for them upon mere seeking.
Śāriputra! These bhikṣus should reflect in this way:
"One must not practice various forms of wrong livelihood or evil dharmas regarding the requisites one needs."
“Śāriputra! If a monk who wears robes made of discarded rags picks up worn-out and tattered pieces from among refuse, he should give rise to this thought:
‘I shall use these to ward off the cold and to cultivate the Noble Path.’”
Because I am now so poor, I have sewn this *saṃghāṭī* to wear and apply myself with diligent effort;
if I were an ordinary person, I should not wear this even for a single night.
That bhikṣu shall wash, sew, and wear it with purity.
If this bhikṣu develops a mind of greedy attachment toward this patched robe, he must immediately discard it; I do not permit him to wear it, much less any other garment.
Why is this? Śāriputra, within these robes, a state that is not that of a bhikṣu has arisen; this bhikṣu should no longer wear them, much less any other objects.
Śāriputra! At such a time, a bhikṣu would rather wrap his body in glowing red-hot iron sheets than wear this hempen robe. Why is that?
Because of the mind of attachment toward this robe.
"Śāriputra, a bhikṣu who wears rag-robes should form this thought: "

"Clad in this hempen robe to ward off cold and heat and to assist in the cultivation of the Path, I shall no longer wear any other garments; I shall attain the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat."
"Śāriputra! For a bhikṣu who wears patched robes and is single-mindedly seeking the Path, I permit him to wear them. Śāriputra!"

A bhikṣu who begs for alms should remain free from conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena; he should always restrain his mind and enter the village without allowing it to become distracted. Adorning himself with various dhyānas and samādhis, he should not let his mind be defiled once he has obtained food. Carrying the food he has received out of the village, he should go to a pure water source or a place suitable for practicing the Path. Setting the food aside, he should wash his feet and sit down, placing the food before him and generating thoughts of revulsion, thoughts of impurity, thoughts of excrement and urine, thoughts of putridity, thoughts of vomit, thoughts of an ointment for a sore, thoughts of loathsomeness, thoughts of the flesh of one's own child, thoughts of a foul fruit, and thoughts of heaviness.
Furthermore, within the body, one should cultivate the perception of birth and death, the perception of blueness, the perception of pus, and the perception of putrefaction.

Śāriputra, a bhikṣu should give rise to such perceptions; only with a mind free from greedy attachment should he then eat, merely to sustain the body, eliminate the ailments of hunger and thirst, and enable him to practice the Way.
One should form this thought:

"By eating this food, I shall destroy prior suffering and distress and not give rise to future suffering; my mind will attain happiness, composure, and freedom from affliction, while my body will become light and agile, and my gait secure."
Again, he thought:
"Having eaten this food, I shall attain the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the fruit of arhat, and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."
"Śāriputra! For a bhikṣu who eats in this manner, I permit begging for food. Śāriputra!"
If a bhikṣu who begs for alms develops a mind of craving for the taste regarding the food he has obtained, considering it sweet and delicious, and thinks:
"By eating this food, I shall obtain a fine complexion and my physical strength shall become abundant."
One should not form this thought:
"I shall diligently practice the Noble Path by eating this food.
Such a bhikṣu, I do not permit him to receive even a single drink of water, let alone a meal.

“Śāriputra! If one eats while failing to perceive the faults and evils within food, and failing to perceive the path leading out [of suffering], it would be better for one to cut off flesh from one’s own thigh with one’s own hand and eat it.”
Why is this? Śāriputra, I permit practitioners and those who have attained realization to receive offerings from others, but I do not permit anyone else. Śāriputra!
What is meant by a "practitioner"?
It refers to a bhikṣu who has made a firm resolve:
"In this present life, I shall sever all fetters and afflictions, and I shall enter nirvana without remainder."
To cultivate the Noble Path as if one’s head were on fire, and furthermore to eradicate unwholesome and evil dharmas—this is called a practitioner.

To be able to single-mindedly believe in and understand emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), in order to attain the fruits of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship (*arhat*) by severing all afflictions—this is called a practitioner.
To seek all wholesome dharmas and constantly practice inquiry—this is called a practitioner.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, one who can resolve to deliver all beings is called a practitioner;

one who diligently cultivates the various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), acts according to what is taught in the sūtras, and single-mindedly seeks the Buddha-way—such a person is a practitioner.
Within the Buddha-dharma, such a person is called a "practitioner.
What is meant by a "realizer"?
One who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna and is liberated from the three evil realms is called a "realizer."

The Sakṛdāgāmin, the Anāgāmin, and the Arhat have severed all afflictions; their seeking for the Path has ceased, they have accomplished what was to be done, and they have well trained in the three trainings—these are called those who have attained.
"I have heard that such a person may receive offerings; if such a person receives offerings, it is called receiving offerings rightly. Śāriputra!"

Those who maintain pure precepts, those who instruct and transform donors, and those who cultivate learning by reciting the sūtras—namely, the *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, and other such scriptures, as well as the *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*—if these persons can also maintain pure precepts without flaw, being untainted, unclouded, autonomous, and unattached; if they are praised by the wise and are self-sufficient, following meditative concentration and delighting from time to time in sitting in dhyāna—such bhikṣus, I likewise permit and accept offerings for.
“Śāriputra! One who has realized the Dharma through bodily witness has no doubt or regret; I permit such a person to preach the Dharma from a high seat.

Although they may be an ordinary person, they maintain pure precepts, their minds do not cling to the doctrines of non-Buddhist scriptures, and they single-mindedly and diligently seek the supreme fruits of the śramaṇa. They do not crave gain or offerings, and they skillfully and definitively teach with extensive learning and vast analogies like the great ocean. Even at the cost of their lives, they do not speak falsely; they take no pleasure in contention, benefiting both themselves and others, and speak only of the pure, foremost, and ultimate truth. What they preach is exactly as they practice.”
"Śāriputra! When one speaks in this manner, I authorize them to preach the Dharma.
What the Tathāgata has taught is such that it causes no contradiction among all dharmas; namely, he teaches morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation."
Śāriputra! A bhikṣu who seeks only profit has left the household life for the sake of the Buddha, yet he breaks the precepts; what use is there in his preaching the Dharma?
Why is this? Śāriputra,
in my sūtras I have said:
"If a person is not themselves well-composed and cannot protect themselves, it is impossible for them to cause others to be well-composed and to protect themselves.
It is like a person who, while submerged in mud themselves, wishes to pull others out; such a thing is impossible."
"If a person can bring themselves to sublime tranquility and emerge from the mire, and then desires to help others emerge as well, such a thing is possible.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I now tell you clearly:

the offense of slandering the Tathāgata is not light. A bhikṣu who speaks the truth should listen to the preaching of the Dharma; it is a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts, not one who speaks falsely, who is able to bestow the gift of the Dharma.
“Śāriputra! To preach the Dharma from a high seat and decisively sever doubts is the most supreme task.
However, if one’s observance of the precepts is impure and they are attached to the doctrines of external paths, I do not permit it.”

Furthermore, I do not permit those who speak falsely, those who prize worldly pleasures, those who seek gain and offerings, or those who delight in disputes and litigation to sit upon the high seat and preach the Dharma.

I permit only those who purely uphold the precepts, those whose minds are upright and sincere, and those who have thoroughly realized the true nature of all phenomena to ascend the high seat and preach the Dharma.

“Śāriputra! A precept-breaking bhikṣu would rather renounce the precepts than, while wearing the saṃghāṭī robe—the mark of a noble one—conceal his defilements and sins, secretly committing various evils while receiving the faithful offerings of others.”
“Śāriputra! Because of a minor cause and condition, one will undergo the body of a hell-being for a vast period of time. Chapter Ten:
Entrustment (Part Two) *The Sūtra on the Treasury of the Buddha*, Chapter Ten: Entrustment At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
At that time, how will those bhikṣus apply themselves with diligence toward wholesome dharmas?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Let this be set aside; do not inquire further. Why is this?
At that time, even the bhikṣus would be unable to believe the sūtras spoken by the Buddha’s immeasurable wisdom, let alone be able to practice them diligently."
Ānanda! All the wisdom that the Tathāgata possesses regarding conditioned phenomena cannot be understood or known by any pratyekabuddhas, arhats, or others.
Ānanda! If the Dharma known by the Tathāgata were to be explained to you, you would become bewildered and distressed; how much less could such a person believe it?

Even now, when the Tathāgata speaks such a sūtra as this, that foolish person still does not believe it; how much less could they believe in the retribution for their offenses that has been described?
Ānanda! Such is the nature of things!

One who is evil himself will call others evil as well. Just as the foremost indolent bhikṣu of the present cannot be matched by the foremost diligent bhikṣu of that time, so too their observed precepts, deportment, and wisdom cannot be compared.

If the Tathāgata were to describe all the transgressions and evils committed by this person, as well as what they will undergo upon changing bodies, these people would not believe it and would instead commit even more grave offenses.
If you yourselves were to hear this, you too would become distressed and fearful, for you could not measure the extent of the evil retribution they will suffer.
Ānanda! Those who receive the profound Dharma of the Tathāgata are rare.
What do you think?
“Would a piglet take pleasure in fine beds and mattresses? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Ānanda! This *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of mine is a dharma that is profound and subtle, which those with wisdom delight in; yet such people are unable to believe, understand, or penetrate it.”

Having gone forth and called himself a śramaṇa, he was unable to endure authentic instruction; within this Dharma, he could not cultivate his mind nor find its flavor, so he shook his hand and departed, falling into the evil realms, just like a piglet abandoning a fine bed and mattress.
Why is this? Ānanda! This *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of mine is profoundly deep and pure; it is not for those who are difficult to transform.
Those who can be brought to faith and understanding; those who are difficult to subdue; those lacking wisdom; those difficult to satisfy;
those difficult to support; those who have broken the precepts; those with whom it is difficult to converse; those dwelling in false teachings; those practicing wrong conduct;
those who prize wealth and profit; those for whom food and clothing are paramount; and those who have violated the rules of decorum.
Those who lack the virtue of precepts, those who have fallen from the summit, the wicked, the indolent, those with small desires,
those with little diligence, the shameless, those who tolerate shame, and those who are preoccupied with busy affairs—
these are the *caṇḍālas* among śramaṇas, the white-robed among śramaṇas, the ruined among śramaṇas.
Those who walk the path of evil within this gateway; those who are not śramaṇas yet claim to be śramaṇas; those swallowed by Māra;
those whose views accord with the tenets of external paths; those who do not practice according to their words; those who delight in the clamor of crowds;
those who delight in idle chatter; those possessed of the works of Māra; those afflicted and distressed by Māra; and those possessed of the afflictions (kleśa).
As for those who are burning with passion— those who hold views of a self, views of a person, views of a sentient being, and those who are inverted—
it is impossible that they could have faith, understanding, or thorough penetration in this Dharma of mine.
Why is this? Ānanda!
My anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is pure, blissful, and vast; it is not compatible with such evil persons.

Ānanda! For example, the vast distance between hundreds of thousands of billions of trichiliocosms is such that even this wicked person is far removed from the Dharma of the śramaṇas; how much more so, then, regarding the attainment of *anulomikī-kṣānti*?
"How much less could they attain nirvana? Ānanda!

Such matters as these cannot be fully described; in the future, there will be śramaṇas who are wicked, evil, and base, who harbor deep greed and avarice, harbor deep anger and hatred, and harbor deep lack of faith."
The three poisons blaze fiercely, and their mental conduct is coarse and wild, making them difficult to restrain.

Ānanda! Suppose, for example, that a fertile field has ripened well but one burns it with fire; or that one consumes sweet and delicious food but ingests poison; or that one’s entire house and possessions are consumed by fire—is this appropriate? Is it not so?
"No, World-Honored One. "Ānanda!"

In this way, foolish people in future ages will receive offerings because they have encountered my Dharma, yet they will lack faith and understanding regarding the Tathāgata’s merits; furthermore, they will be unable to believe such sūtras as these, and being incapable of enduring a truthful critique of their faults, they will recognize their own sores and wounds while going against my words.
Such deluded people rely on the Buddha for their livelihood, yet they act in opposition to this Dharma. Ānanda!
At that time, Jambudvīpa will be filled with such deluded people.
Ānanda! Let it be.
What is the use of seeking out this foolish and evil person, who performs such wicked deeds in vain and in the waste of his life?
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should this sutra be named?”
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'The Buddha-Treasury,' and it is also named 'Arousing Diligence,' also named 'Subduing the Violation of Precepts,' and also named 'Discerning All Dharmas.'"
"You should uphold it.
Ānanda! If anyone recites and upholds this sutra, the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless."
Why is this? A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts cannot even believe in, recite, or teach others; how much less could he find a heart of joy therein?
For what reason?
Ānanda! It is just as when a wicked thief, out of fear of the king or his ministers, does not dare to reveal himself while stealing another's property and does not call himself a thief.
Even so, Ānanda!

A bhikṣu who has broken the precepts and has become established in non-śramaṇa conduct does not even say of himself that he is evil, much less can he speak to others, saying of himself, "I am a sinner."

Ānanda! When bhikṣus who have broken the precepts hear such a sutra as this, they will be able to subdue themselves and possess a sense of shame; bhikṣus who uphold the precepts will cause their own virtue to increase.

While this sutra was being spoken, countless devas attained the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. Māra the Evil One and his retinue were all deeply distressed, as if they had fallen into sixteen great pits; they wailed loudly, saying:

"The śramaṇa Gautama knows me and awakens me! For a long night, I have constantly wished that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who uphold the precepts would be destroyed and those who break the precepts would be assisted, so that evil bhikṣus would not know the Buddha-dharma but would only know how to recite it."
I intended to shatter the sense of security within the Buddha’s Dharma by declaring that this is not the Buddha’s Dharma and lacks any meaningful purpose.
Yet, Gautama, amidst this great assembly of devas, humans, and others, now protects this Dharma and thwarts my wish.
After Māra had spoken these words, he was overcome with grief and distress and suddenly vanished.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this matter, spoke these verses:
“The various dharmas I have taught accord with the ultimate truth;”
Conditioned things are not solid, like what is seen in a dream.
I now preach this Dharma to censure future events;
following the ultimate truth, it restrains all evil persons.
At that time, in the evil world, the minds of bhikṣus will be agitated;
disputes will give rise to right and wrong, and they shall not attain nirvāṇa.
Whether śramaṇas or laypeople, what they speak will be no different [from the truth].
At that time, this Dharma of mine was no different from worldly dharmas;
for the sake of householders, I said:
"You should know me as rare."
"I have attained the Dharma of the Buddha; I have realized the first fruit of the initial path.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu said:
"What I say is no different from this."
"This person is the same as I; I am truly one who has seen the Dharma.
Thus, those who have seen the Dharma and those who have not, for the sake of laypeople, each give rise to their own debates within their respective doctrines.
Some say that all exists; others say that all is empty.
Not abiding in the True Path, their evil nature destroys my Dharma.
"Do not associate with such people; you should come and draw near to me."
"I shall preach the True Dharma for you, so that you may quickly attain the Way as I have.
Such voices as these spread far and wide;
with like-minded factions supporting one another, they destroy my teaching of the Dharma.
Just as various evil bandits, Associating with one another in their wickedness,
Rebel against and destroy the kingdom, Its cities, towns, and villages; At that time,
the bhikṣus Will be difficult to transform and instruct.
With dull faculties and deep-seated attachments, possessing little wisdom, they rely on the notions of self and person.
Failing to understand the Tathāgata’s teachings given according to what is appropriate,
they speak of the increase of outflows while claiming for themselves that they have attained the Way.
Within this great assembly, there are many bhikṣus;
all claim to possess wisdom, yet not one seeks true knowledge.
If within this great assembly there should be even a single bhikṣu...
Those who possess wisdom as it truly is all reproach him, saying he lacks wisdom.
When the devas and other celestial beings see that the Way of the Dharma King has crumbled and perished,
they are all filled with sorrow and distress, weeping as they face one another.
Among them were tree deities who fell from their trees to the ground,
all saying:
"The Lion of the Śākyas' sublime Dharma is now utterly destroyed."
The Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha have not yet been in the world for long;
how is it that today they shall all be dispersed and destroyed?
We shall no longer hear the teachings spoken by the Tathāgata.
"Enshrouded in the darkness of ignorance and knowing nothing, the Supreme Path is now about to perish.
At that time, all the earth-deities raised a great cry:
"The Great Dharma-torch of the Tathāgata shall now be extinguished!"
"O devas and all spirits, do not later feel regret and say that you neither saw nor heard it,
for the Way of the Buddha has now perished.
Over immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata has benefited himself and benefited others.
Enduring all manner of suffering and affliction, he made the vow to attain Buddhahood.
Now that the Great Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, who delivers all sentient beings,
is about to pass away, the pure and subtle Dharma is likewise on the verge of total extinction.
These foolish and evil thieves shall now gain their power;
devoid of any heart of compassion, they will slander, revile, and harass one another.
The emissaries of Māra and the subjects of Māra possess dull faculties that are difficult to transform.
With a mind of flattery, crookedness, and indolence, and with hatred that destroys the Buddha-dharma,
one merely sits in meditation in an empty forest for three full months;
yet to claim oneself is an Arhat— without dhyāna, how could one have attained the Way?
They claim to have attained the Way, yet upon death they say they have entered nirvana;
the multitude, believing them, erects stupas for them, while they themselves enter hell.
Such fools, empty of virtue, treat one another with mutual contempt and anger.
"What I have attained over immeasurable kalpas is now utterly destroyed.
At that time, the deities of space, together beholding the Lion of the Śākyas,
cried out in lamentation as the sublime Dharma was being ruined and brought to ruin.
When the Four Heavenly Kings heard this, they were all filled with anxiety and distress;
together with the various celestial deities, they all descended at that time.
To the city of Alakāvatī, the hosts of yakṣa spirits came.
All of them wept bitterly, producing terrifying sounds.
There were cities made of the seven treasures, exquisitely adorned and most subtle;
yet their splendor now faded like common earth, and the devas took no pleasure in dwelling there.
Wailing with great lamentation, they gathered from every quarter;
each harbored grief and distress, unable to speak even upon meeting one another.
Lying prostrate upon the ground, they uttered such sounds as these:
Traversing together through Jambudvīpa, we behold this great terror:
the sons of the Buddha engaging in strife and contention, destroying the Dharma and dispersing;
all having come from the heavens, they have gathered together at my place of birth.
The divine palaces made of various jewels lost their radiance for seven days;
the gods sat together weeping, remaining without rising for the full seven days, saying:
"How is it that he of great diligence, the courageous World-Honored One!"
"We saw you dwelling here, but now we shall never see you again.
Together they went to the Jetavana and wept as they faced one another, saying:
"The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths here, and it was here that we heard them."
The world is about to fall into blindness and darkness; They will mutually despise, resent, and be arrogant toward one another;
Merely giving rise to various evil karmas, They shall return and fall into the evil realms.
The wondrous palaces of the devas— How lamentable that they are now about to become empty!
"We, the various devas, have no one left to save us.
At that time, Jambudvīpa was ruined and its majestic splendor vanished;
beneath the trees where they used to walk and meditate, and within the mountain caves, there were no more virtuous people.
All the worlds were utterly and greatly shaken;
the gods and great deities raised sounds of terrifying dread.
At that time, the Trāyastriṃśa gods raised their hands and wept with great compassion.
Within each of their palaces, they raised their voices and wailed;
throughout all the celestial palaces, they all uttered these words:
"We are forever separated from the Great Sage King, who used to preach the Dharma for us."
For six months in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they did not partake of sudhā food;
they heard no sound of music and were filled with grief as if they had lost a son.
When the hosts of asuras heard of such matters, [they were moved].
They all summoned one another to assemble, desiring to attack the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, the kings of Jambudvīpa all joined together to wage war and punish one another;
the devas and asuras likewise all engaged in battle.
At that time, many bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs fell into the evil realms, with only a few escaping;
laypeople who had broken the precepts followed after those evil bhikṣus.
For these reasons, they all head toward the evil realms.
Because these wicked upāsikās follow evil teachers,
they likewise enter the evil realms, causing the entire world to be agitated.
Some enter cities and villages; some go into the mountain forests;
harboring anxiety and distress in their hearts as they travel east and west, they diminish their own lifespans.
At that time, there will be many wicked bandits and many perilous paths.
The five grains do not grow; even if they do grow, they are devoured by insects.
At that time, the people of the world will suffer from famine and many will die of hunger;
having died, they fall among the hungry ghosts (preta), where they endure various sufferings for a long time.
If people of that time should take property given to the Buddha, to a stūpa, or to the Saṅgha of the four quarters,
and immediately divide and consume it all among themselves, the Saṅgha will be like this after my passing.
Ānanda, you and the others should exert yourselves with diligent vigor.
Do not see such various evils in the future final age.
All ordinary worldlings, being foolish and lacking wisdom,
give rise to the karma of ordinary beings and swiftly fall into the evil realms.
"You should diligently recite and chant; this is called the cause of wisdom.
If for the sake of wisdom, you will swiftly reach the supreme state.
I have studied the right view of the world; you should study as I have."
Severing worldly obstacles, one will swiftly reach the supreme state.
Diligently practicing the Noble Eightfold Path, one shall quickly attain Nirvana;
contemplating and seeking one's own benefit—this is what I have taught.
After this kalpa has passed, for sixty kalpas there will be no Buddha;
there will not even be the sound of a Buddha’s voice, let alone anyone who attains the Way.
At that time, the people of the world will be tormented by hunger and starvation.
Lacking any heart of filial piety or compassion, they eat their mothers and the flesh of their children.
Whenever families give birth to sons, they constantly guard them for fear that others might eat them.
Who, upon hearing of such evil deeds, would ever again give rise to the karma of birth and death?
All sufferings have ignorance as their root; the five aggregates have craving as their root.
If one does not delight in the five desires, one should sever all attachments.
When receiving the retribution of meritorious fruits, a mind of deep attachment arises.
Due to the causes and conditions of craving and attachment, one gives rise to evil and falls into the miserable realms.
The untainted Dharma is empty and quiescent; in this world, nothing is firm or enduring.
If you know this to be so, you all should act with haste.
Without a mind, they give rise to thoughts in their minds, and thus become greatly startled and afraid: "Am I doing it or not?
What is the nature of this matter?"
Thus these ordinary worldlings, reflecting and deliberating,
"How shall I act? constantly weep in this manner.
Where there are no aggregates, they conceive the notion of aggregates; where there is no self, they conceive the notion of a self.
Upon hearing the teaching that intrinsic characteristics are empty, they likewise become bewildered and distressed.
They do not understand the Buddha’s teaching on the reality of the aggregates as they truly are.
Hearing this, they take it for certain; they perceive fear where there is no fear.
I declare that the aggregates of the past, future, and present are all empty and quiescent;
the three times are entirely equal, just like space.
All Buddhas of the past Also taught that self-characteristics are empty;
All Buddhas of the future Also teach that self-characteristics are empty.
I, now appearing in the world, Also teach that all dharmas [are empty].
The intrinsic nature and specific characteristics are empty; they do not differ across the three periods of time.
Those of the future will not know the true meaning taught by the Buddha;
clinging greedily to a self and sentient beings, they constantly fall into the evil realms.
"In the future age it shall be thus; the great evils will be most fearsome.
You all must exert yourselves with diligent vigor; do not witness such a degenerate world.

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Śāriputra, the various bhikṣus, and the entire assembly of devas, humans, and others in the world, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced and faithfully accepted the Buddha’s words.
